Thus the proof of reason and the proof of transmission have become clear to you, and God's proof has been established against you.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your mention﴾, that he said: "Your honor." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: "In it is your news." In another report from him he said: "In it is your religion."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, through the route of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "God sent a prophet from Himyar called Shu'ayb. A servant (of the king) leapt at him and struck him with a staff. Bukhtanassar then marched against them, fought them, and killed them until none of them remained. And concerning them God revealed ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ to His saying ﴿extinguished﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Kalbi regarding His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ that he said: "It is the town of Hadur, of the Azd." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿and return to that in which you were given luxury﴾ that he said: "Return to your homes and your wealth."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿and that claim of theirs did not cease﴾ that he said: "They are the people of Hadur who had killed their prophet, so God sent Bukhtanassar against them and he killed them." And regarding His saying ﴿We made them as harvested crops, extinguished﴾ he said: "With the sword; the angels struck their faces until they returned to their dwellings."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Wahb, who said: "A man from the people of al-Jazar related to me: Yemen was two towns, one called Hadur and the other Qilabah. They became insolent and were given luxury, until they did not even close their doors. When they had been given luxury, God sent them a prophet who called them, but they killed him. So God put into the heart of Bukhtanassar that he should attack them, and he equipped an army for them. They fought them, and they defeated his army, so they returned to him in defeat. He then equipped against them a second army, larger than the first, and they defeated them too. When Bukhtanassar saw this, he went out to fight them himself, and they fought him, and he defeated them until they fled out of the town running. They heard a caller calling, ﴿Do not run, but return to that in which you were given luxury and to your dwellings﴾, so they returned. Then they heard a voice calling, 'O vengeance for the Prophet!' and they were killed by the sword. This is what God referred to in His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ to His saying 'extinguished'."

I say: The villages of Hadur are well known today, between them and the city of Sana'a, about one *barid* (a unit of distance) to the west of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿harvested crops, extinguished﴾ that he said: "Like the extinguishing of fire when it is put out." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ that he said: "The pastime is a child." Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ that he said: "The women." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and they do not tire﴾ that he said: "They do not return." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ that he said: "about His servants," ﴿but they will be questioned﴾, he said: "about their deeds." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded a similar report from al-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is no people on earth more hateful to me than the Qadariyyah (a sect that denied divine predestination), and that is only because they do not know the power of God." God says, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾.

He drew His servants' attention to the greatness of His favor upon them by His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿In which is your remembrance﴾ is a description of "a Book." The "remembrance" here means honor: that is, in it is your honor, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a remembrance for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. It was also said: "In it is your remembrance" means the mention of the matter of your religion, the rulings of your law, and what you will attain of reward or punishment. It was also said: "In it is your story." This was said by Mujahid. It was said: "In it are the noble qualities of your character and the excellence of your deeds." It was said: "In it is acting upon what your life depends on." This was said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah. It was said: "In it is your admonition." The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach: that is, "Will you not reason that the matter is so?" or "Will you not reason about any of the things of which these are part?"

Then He threatened them and warned them of what befell the nations that denied, saying: ﴿And how many a town did We destroy, which had been wrongdoing﴾. The word "kam" (how many) is in the accusative position, as the object of "qasamna" (We destroyed). It is the informative "kam," which indicates multiplicity. Qasm means breaking and crushing something. It is said: "I broke the back of so-and-so" when you broke it, and "his tooth broke" when it was shattered. The meaning here is destruction and punishment. As for fasm with the letter fa', it means a split in a thing without separation. The clause ﴿which had been wrongdoing﴾ is in the genitive position as a description of "town." In the speech there is an omitted noun: that is, "And how many a town's people did We destroy, who were wrongdoers," meaning disbelievers in Allah, denying His signs. Wrongdoing (zulm) originally means placing a thing in other than its place, and they placed disbelief in the place of faith. ﴿And We brought into being after them another people﴾: that is, We created and produced, after the destruction of its people, a people who were not of them.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾: that is, they realized or saw Our punishment. Al-Akhfash said: they feared and anticipated it. Or "might" (ba's) means severe punishment. ﴿Behold, they were fleeing from it﴾. Rakd (fleeing) means running away, escaping and being routed. Its origin is from "rakada al-rajul al-dabbah" (the man spurred the mount with his legs). It is said "rakada al-faras" when he urged the horse on with his shanks. Then it became common until it was said "rakada al-faras" when it ran. From the same root is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The meaning is that they fled from it, spurring their mounts. Then it was said to them: ﴿Do not flee﴾, that is, do not run away. It was said that the angels called out to them at the time of their flight. It was also said that those who said it to them were those present there from among the believers, mocking them and deriding them.

﴿And return to what you were made to enjoy of luxury and your dwellings﴾: that is, return to your blessings which were the cause of your insolence and disbelief. The mutraf is the one made to enjoy blessings; it is said "utrifa fulan," meaning he was given abundance in his livelihood. ﴿And your dwellings﴾: that is, return to your dwellings which you used to inhabit and boast of. ﴿Perhaps you will be questioned﴾: that is, you will be sought out to be asked and consulted and to plan regarding important matters. This is in the manner of mockery toward them and rebuke of them. It was also said: the meaning is "perhaps you will be asked about what punishment has befallen you, so you will inform about it." It was also said: "perhaps you will be asked to believe, as you used to be asked that before the punishment came upon you."

The commentators and the scholars of reports said: the intended people of this verse are the people of Hadur from Yemen. Allah, glorified is He, had sent to them a prophet named Shu'ayb ibn Muhaddam, whose grave is on one of the mountains of Yemen called Din, and between it and Hadur is about a postal distance. They said: he is not Shu'ayb, companion of Madyan. I say: the traces of the grave on the mountain of Din exist, and the common people of that region claim that it is the grave of Qudum ibn Qadim.

﴿They said: "O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ That is, when the angels said to them "Do not flee," they said: "O woe to us," that is, [they cried out] for our destruction: "Indeed we were wrongdoers," being wrongdoers to ourselves, deserving punishment for what we had sent forward. So they acknowledged against themselves the wrongdoing that necessitated punishment.

﴿And that remained their cry﴾: that is, this word remained their cry, meaning their call. The word is their saying "O woe to us!" That is, they called out with it and repeated it. ﴿Until We made them as cut stubble﴾: that is, with swords, as grain is harvested by the sickle. Hasid here means "mahsud" (reaped). The meaning of ﴿extinguished﴾ is that they were dead, from "khamadat al-nar" (the fire went out) when it was extinguished. So the extinction of life is compared to the extinction of fire, as it is said of one who has died: "he has been extinguished."

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾: that is, We did not create them in vain or for nothing, but to alert to the fact that they have a creator, capable, whose command must be obeyed. In this there is a general indication of the creation of the world. What is meant by "what is between them" is all the creatures existing between the heaven and the earth, despite the variety of their kinds and the diversity of their species.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: lahw is what one amuses oneself with. It was said: lahw is wife and child; it was said: wife alone; it was said: child alone. Al-Jawhari said: lahw is sometimes used as a euphemism for intercourse. What he said is supported by the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Did not Basbasah claim today that I have grown old and that people like me cannot enjoy pastime?

And from the same is the saying of another:

And among them is a pastime for the friend, and a sight.

The clause is a new sentence confirming the content of what precedes it. The answer to "law" (if) is His saying: ﴿We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾: that is, from Our presence and by Our power, not from yourselves. The commentators said: that is, from the Houris of paradise. In this there is a refutation of those who say that a wife and child are ascribed to Allah, exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. It was also said: it intends to refute those who said: the idols or the angels are the daughters of Allah. Ibn Qutaybah said: the verse is a refutation of the Christians.

﴿If We were doing [it]﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: "ma kunna fa'ilin" (we were not doing). Al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that "in" (if) is negative as the commentators mentioned: that is, We did not do that and did not take a wife or child. It is also permissible that it is conditional: that is, if We were of those who do that, We would have taken it from Ourselves. Al-Farra' said: this is the more likely of the two views according to the school of Arabic grammar.

﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it﴾. This is a turning away from the adoption of play: that is, leave that which they say, for it is a lie and falsehood. Rather, Our way is to hurl the truth upon falsehood, so it crushes it, that is, overpowers it. The origin of "damgh" is splitting the head until it reaches the brain, and from it comes "al-damigha" (the crushing calamity). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that We remove it, removing it with the removal of humiliation and disgrace, since its origin is hitting the brain with a blow.

It was said: by "the truth" is meant the proof (hujjah). Ahh. And by "falsehood" their doubts. It was said: the truth is admonitions and falsehood is sins. It was said: falsehood is Satan. It was said: their lie and their describing Allah, glorified is He, with attributes not His.

﴿So then it is vanishing﴾: that is, it is departing and going away. It was said: it is perishing and destroyed. The meanings are close, and "idha" here is the sudden "idha" (then suddenly).

﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾: that is, punishment in the Hereafter because of your describing Him with what is not befitting for Him. It was said: "woe" is a valley in Hell. It is a warning to Quraysh that for them is a punishment like that of those people. The "min" in "mimma" is causal (because of).

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, as slaves and possession. He is their creator, their provider and their owner. How then could it be permissible for some of His creatures to be partners to Him, worshipped as He is worshipped? This sentence confirms what precedes it. ﴿And those near Him﴾ means the angels. In it is a refutation of those who say the angels are the daughters of Allah. In describing them as being near Him there is an indication of their honor and nobility, and that they are in the position of the close attendants of kings. Then He described them with His saying: ﴿They do not disdain to worship Him﴾: that is, they do not consider themselves too great nor refuse to worship Allah, glorified is He, and to humble themselves before Him. ﴿Nor do they grow weary﴾: that is, they do not tire. It is derived from "hasir," which is a camel that has stopped from exhaustion and fatigue. It is said: "hasara al-ba'ir yahsuru husuran" (the camel became exhausted and tired). "Istahsara" and "tahassara" are similar, and "hasartuhu" I made him weary, transitive and intransitive. Abu Zayd said: they do not tire. Ibn al-A'rabi said: they do not lose heart. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is that these whom you mentioned as children of Allah are the servants of Allah; they do not refuse His worship nor consider themselves too great for it, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 206]. It was also said: the meaning is that they do not cease from His worship. These meanings are close.

﴿They glorify [Him] night and day; they do not slacken﴾: that is, they declare Allah free of imperfection, constantly, without weakening in that or growing tired. It was said: they pray night and day. Al-Zajjaj said: the course of glorification from them is like the course of breath from us; nothing distracts us from breathing, so their glorification is constant. This sentence is either a new sentence answering an implied question, or in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth [who can] raise the dead?﴾ Al-Mufaddal said: the purpose of this interrogation is denial: that is, they have not taken gods able to give life. "Am" here is the disjunctive "am," and the hamza is for denying occurrence. Al-Mubarrad said: "am" here has the meaning of "hal" (is it that): that is, have these polytheists taken gods from the earth who give life to the dead? "Am" here cannot mean "bal" (rather), because that would imply that they can create the dead, unless "am" is taken as accompanied by an interrogative, making it the disjunctive "am," and then the meaning is sound. "Min al-ard" (from the earth) is connected to "ittakhadhu" (took), or to an omitted word which is a description of "gods." The meaning of "they raise" is they resurrect the dead. The clause is a description of "gods." This clause is what the denial and ignorance-attribution revolve around, not the taking itself, since that takes place from them without doubt. The meaning: "Rather, they have taken gods from the earth, [gods] who alone, despite their lowliness, raise the dead." But that is not the case, for those they took as gods are far from that. Al-Jumhur read "yunshirun" with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the shin, from "anshara-hu," meaning "ahyahu" (gave him life). Al-Hasan read it with a fathah on the ya': that is, "yahyawna wa-la yamutun" (they live and do not die).

Then He, glorified is He, established proof of the invalidity of multiple gods, saying: ﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾: that is, had there been in the heavens and the earth gods worshipped other than Allah, they would have been ruined, meaning they would have been corrupted, namely the heavens and the earth with what is in them of creatures. Al-Kisa'i, Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and the majority of grammarians said: "illa" here is not for exception but means "ghayr" (other than), a description of "gods." That is why the noun after it was in the nominative and the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of "ghayr" appeared in it, since "illa" here has the meaning of "ghayr." From it is the saying of the poet:

And every brother whose brother departs from him, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads [i.e., they do not depart].

Al-Farra' said: "illa" here means "siwa" (other than): the meaning being: had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined. The reason for ruin is that the existence of another god with Allah necessitates that each of them be capable of independent control of management, so conflict and disagreement occur, and corruption is caused by it. End.

﴿So glorified is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾. The "fa" (so) is to order what follows upon what precedes, from the establishment of oneness by proof: that is, He is exalted, mighty and majestic, above what is not befitting for Him, such as the existence of a partner for Him. In this is guidance for the servants to declare the Lord, glorified is He, free of what is not befitting for Him.

﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾. This sentence is a new sentence explaining that He, glorified is He, because of the strength of His authority and the greatness of His majesty, is not asked by any of His creatures about any of His decree and destiny. ﴿But they will be questioned﴾, that is, the servants will be questioned about what they do; Allah will question them about that because they are His servants. It was also said: the meaning is that He, glorified is He, is not held accountable for His actions, while they are held accountable. It was said: the intended meaning is that He, glorified is He, made clear to His servants that whoever is questioned about his deeds, like the Messiah and the angels, is not suitable to be a god.

(p-933) ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ That is, "Rather, they have taken," and this is a shift (*idrab*) and a move from demonstrating the falsehood of their being gods by the preceding proof to demonstrating the falsehood of taking them as gods, while rebuking them by demanding proof from them. For this reason He said, ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ for the claim that they are gods, or for the permissibility of taking gods other than God. They have no way to any such thing, neither through reason (*'aql*) nor through transmitted evidence (*naql*). The proof of reason has already been explained, and as for the proof of transmission, He indicated it in His saying: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾. That is: this revelation concerning monotheism, which contains the decisive proof, is the reminder of my community and the reminder of the earlier nations. I have established it against you and made it clear to you, so you establish your proof. It was also said that the meaning is: this Qur'an and these earlier books that were sent down before me. Look and see whether in any one of them God commanded taking any god besides Him. Al-Zajjaj said: they were told, "Bring your proof that some messenger among the messengers informed his community that they have a god other than God. Is the mention of those with me and those before me anything but the oneness of God?" It was also said that the meaning of the speech is warning and threat, that is: do whatever you wish, for soon the veil will be lifted.

Abu Hatim related that Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "هذا ذكرٌ من معي وذكرٌ من قبلي" with tanwin on both *dhikr* words and with a kasra on the *mim* of *min*, and he claimed that there is no basis for this reading. Al-Zajjaj, in explaining this reading, said that the meaning is: "This is a reminder of what has been revealed to me and what is with me, and the reminder of those before me." It was also said: a reminder existing from before me, that is, I have brought what the prophets before me brought.

Then, when the proof was directed at them, He censured them for their ignorance of the places of truth, saying: ﴿Rather, most of them do not know the truth﴾. This is a shift (*idrab*) on His part, glorified is He, and a move from reproaching them by demanding proof to explaining that the establishment of proof does not affect them, because they are ignorant of the truth and cannot distinguish it from falsehood. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Hasan read *al-haqq* with a *damma* (as *al-haqqu*), in the sense of "this is the truth," or "it is the truth." The clause ﴿so they are turning away﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, namely that most of them do not know. That is: because of this ignorance that prevails over most of them, they are turning away from accepting the truth, persisting in turning away from monotheism and from following the Messenger. Therefore they do not consider any argument, nor reflect on any proof, nor ponder any evidence.

﴿We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me.﴾ Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *nuhi* with the *nun*, while the rest read it with the *ya'*, that is, "We reveal to him." And in this is an affirmation of the matter of monotheism and an emphasis on what came earlier in His saying: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾. He concluded the verse with the command to His servants to worship Him, saying ﴿so worship Me﴾. Thus the proof of reason and the proof of transmission have become clear to you, and God's proof has been established against you.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your mention﴾, that he said: "Your honor." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: "In it is your news." In another report from him he said: "In it is your religion."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, through the route of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "God sent a prophet from Himyar called Shu'ayb. A servant (of the king) leapt at him and struck him with a staff. Bukhtanassar then marched against them, fought them, and killed them until none of them remained. And concerning them God revealed ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ to His saying ﴿extinguished﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Kalbi regarding His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ that he said: "It is the town of Hadur, of the Azd." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿and return to that in which you were given luxury﴾ that he said: "Return to your homes and your wealth."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿and that claim of theirs did not cease﴾ that he said: "They are the people of Hadur who had killed their prophet, so God sent Bukhtanassar against them and he killed them." And regarding His saying ﴿We made them as harvested crops, extinguished﴾ he said: "With the sword; the angels struck their faces until they returned to their dwellings."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Wahb, who said: "A man from the people of al-Jazar related to me: Yemen was two towns, one called Hadur and the other Qilabah. They became insolent and were given luxury, until they did not even close their doors. When they had been given luxury, God sent them a prophet who called them, but they killed him. So God put into the heart of Bukhtanassar that he should attack them, and he equipped an army for them. They fought them, and they defeated his army, so they returned to him in defeat. He then equipped against them a second army, larger than the first, and they defeated them too. When Bukhtanassar saw this, he went out to fight them himself, and they fought him, and he defeated them until they fled out of the town running. They heard a caller calling, ﴿Do not run, but return to that in which you were given luxury and to your dwellings﴾, so they returned. Then they heard a voice calling, 'O vengeance for the Prophet!' and they were killed by the sword. This is what God referred to in His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ to His saying 'extinguished'."

I say: The villages of Hadur are well known today, between them and the city of Sana'a, about one *barid* (a unit of distance) to the west of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿harvested crops, extinguished﴾ that he said: "Like the extinguishing of fire when it is put out." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ that he said: "The pastime is a child." Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ that he said: "The women." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and they do not tire﴾ that he said: "They do not return." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ that he said: "about His servants," ﴿but they will be questioned﴾, he said: "about their deeds." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded a similar report from al-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is no people on earth more hateful to me than the Qadariyyah (a sect that denied divine predestination), and that is only because they do not know the power of God." God says, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾.

He drew His servants' attention to the greatness of His favor upon them by His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿In which is your remembrance﴾ is a description of "a Book." The "remembrance" here means honor: that is, in it is your honor, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a remembrance for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. It was also said: "In it is your remembrance" means the mention of the matter of your religion, the rulings of your law, and what you will attain of reward or punishment. It was also said: "In it is your story." This was said by Mujahid. It was said: "In it are the noble qualities of your character and the excellence of your deeds." It was said: "In it is acting upon what your life depends on." This was said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah. It was said: "In it is your admonition." The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach: that is, "Will you not reason that the matter is so?" or "Will you not reason about any of the things of which these are part?"

Then He threatened them and warned them of what befell the nations that denied, saying: ﴿And how many a town did We destroy, which had been wrongdoing﴾. The word "kam" (how many) is in the accusative position, as the object of "qasamna" (We destroyed). It is the informative "kam," which indicates multiplicity. Qasm means breaking and crushing something. It is said: "I broke the back of so-and-so" when you broke it, and "his tooth broke" when it was shattered. The meaning here is destruction and punishment. As for fasm with the letter fa', it means a split in a thing without separation. The clause ﴿which had been wrongdoing﴾ is in the genitive position as a description of "town." In the speech there is an omitted noun: that is, "And how many a town's people did We destroy, who were wrongdoers," meaning disbelievers in Allah, denying His signs. Wrongdoing (zulm) originally means placing a thing in other than its place, and they placed disbelief in the place of faith. ﴿And We brought into being after them another people﴾: that is, We created and produced, after the destruction of its people, a people who were not of them.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾: that is, they realized or saw Our punishment. Al-Akhfash said: they feared and anticipated it. Or "might" (ba's) means severe punishment. ﴿Behold, they were fleeing from it﴾. Rakd (fleeing) means running away, escaping and being routed. Its origin is from "rakada al-rajul al-dabbah" (the man spurred the mount with his legs). It is said "rakada al-faras" when he urged the horse on with his shanks. Then it became common until it was said "rakada al-faras" when it ran. From the same root is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The meaning is that they fled from it, spurring their mounts. Then it was said to them: ﴿Do not flee﴾, that is, do not run away. It was said that the angels called out to them at the time of their flight. It was also said that those who said it to them were those present there from among the believers, mocking them and deriding them.

﴿And return to what you were made to enjoy of luxury and your dwellings﴾: that is, return to your blessings which were the cause of your insolence and disbelief. The mutraf is the one made to enjoy blessings; it is said "utrifa fulan," meaning he was given abundance in his livelihood. ﴿And your dwellings﴾: that is, return to your dwellings which you used to inhabit and boast of. ﴿Perhaps you will be questioned﴾: that is, you will be sought out to be asked and consulted and to plan regarding important matters. This is in the manner of mockery toward them and rebuke of them. It was also said: the meaning is "perhaps you will be asked about what punishment has befallen you, so you will inform about it." It was also said: "perhaps you will be asked to believe, as you used to be asked that before the punishment came upon you."

The commentators and the scholars of reports said: the intended people of this verse are the people of Hadur from Yemen. Allah, glorified is He, had sent to them a prophet named Shu'ayb ibn Muhaddam, whose grave is on one of the mountains of Yemen called Din, and between it and Hadur is about a postal distance. They said: he is not Shu'ayb, companion of Madyan. I say: the traces of the grave on the mountain of Din exist, and the common people of that region claim that it is the grave of Qudum ibn Qadim.

﴿They said: "O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ That is, when the angels said to them "Do not flee," they said: "O woe to us," that is, [they cried out] for our destruction: "Indeed we were wrongdoers," being wrongdoers to ourselves, deserving punishment for what we had sent forward. So they acknowledged against themselves the wrongdoing that necessitated punishment.

﴿And that remained their cry﴾: that is, this word remained their cry, meaning their call. The word is their saying "O woe to us!" That is, they called out with it and repeated it. ﴿Until We made them as cut stubble﴾: that is, with swords, as grain is harvested by the sickle. Hasid here means "mahsud" (reaped). The meaning of ﴿extinguished﴾ is that they were dead, from "khamadat al-nar" (the fire went out) when it was extinguished. So the extinction of life is compared to the extinction of fire, as it is said of one who has died: "he has been extinguished."

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾: that is, We did not create them in vain or for nothing, but to alert to the fact that they have a creator, capable, whose command must be obeyed. In this there is a general indication of the creation of the world. What is meant by "what is between them" is all the creatures existing between the heaven and the earth, despite the variety of their kinds and the diversity of their species.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: lahw is what one amuses oneself with. It was said: lahw is wife and child; it was said: wife alone; it was said: child alone. Al-Jawhari said: lahw is sometimes used as a euphemism for intercourse. What he said is supported by the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Did not Basbasah claim today that I have grown old and that people like me cannot enjoy pastime?

And from the same is the saying of another:

And among them is a pastime for the friend, and a sight.

The clause is a new sentence confirming the content of what precedes it. The answer to "law" (if) is His saying: ﴿We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾: that is, from Our presence and by Our power, not from yourselves. The commentators said: that is, from the Houris of paradise. In this there is a refutation of those who say that a wife and child are ascribed to Allah, exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. It was also said: it intends to refute those who said: the idols or the angels are the daughters of Allah. Ibn Qutaybah said: the verse is a refutation of the Christians.

﴿If We were doing [it]﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: "ma kunna fa'ilin" (we were not doing). Al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that "in" (if) is negative as the commentators mentioned: that is, We did not do that and did not take a wife or child. It is also permissible that it is conditional: that is, if We were of those who do that, We would have taken it from Ourselves. Al-Farra' said: this is the more likely of the two views according to the school of Arabic grammar.

﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it﴾. This is a turning away from the adoption of play: that is, leave that which they say, for it is a lie and falsehood. Rather, Our way is to hurl the truth upon falsehood, so it crushes it, that is, overpowers it. The origin of "damgh" is splitting the head until it reaches the brain, and from it comes "al-damigha" (the crushing calamity). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that We remove it, removing it with the removal of humiliation and disgrace, since its origin is hitting the brain with a blow.

It was said: by "the truth" is meant the proof (hujjah). Ahh. And by "falsehood" their doubts. It was said: the truth is admonitions and falsehood is sins. It was said: falsehood is Satan. It was said: their lie and their describing Allah, glorified is He, with attributes not His.

﴿So then it is vanishing﴾: that is, it is departing and going away. It was said: it is perishing and destroyed. The meanings are close, and "idha" here is the sudden "idha" (then suddenly).

﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾: that is, punishment in the Hereafter because of your describing Him with what is not befitting for Him. It was said: "woe" is a valley in Hell. It is a warning to Quraysh that for them is a punishment like that of those people. The "min" in "mimma" is causal (because of).

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, as slaves and possession. He is their creator, their provider and their owner. How then could it be permissible for some of His creatures to be partners to Him, worshipped as He is worshipped? This sentence confirms what precedes it. ﴿And those near Him﴾ means the angels. In it is a refutation of those who say the angels are the daughters of Allah. In describing them as being near Him there is an indication of their honor and nobility, and that they are in the position of the close attendants of kings. Then He described them with His saying: ﴿They do not disdain to worship Him﴾: that is, they do not consider themselves too great nor refuse to worship Allah, glorified is He, and to humble themselves before Him. ﴿Nor do they grow weary﴾: that is, they do not tire. It is derived from "hasir," which is a camel that has stopped from exhaustion and fatigue. It is said: "hasara al-ba'ir yahsuru husuran" (the camel became exhausted and tired). "Istahsara" and "tahassara" are similar, and "hasartuhu" I made him weary, transitive and intransitive. Abu Zayd said: they do not tire. Ibn al-A'rabi said: they do not lose heart. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is that these whom you mentioned as children of Allah are the servants of Allah; they do not refuse His worship nor consider themselves too great for it, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 206]. It was also said: the meaning is that they do not cease from His worship. These meanings are close.

﴿They glorify [Him] night and day; they do not slacken﴾: that is, they declare Allah free of imperfection, constantly, without weakening in that or growing tired. It was said: they pray night and day. Al-Zajjaj said: the course of glorification from them is like the course of breath from us; nothing distracts us from breathing, so their glorification is constant. This sentence is either a new sentence answering an implied question, or in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth [who can] raise the dead?﴾ Al-Mufaddal said: the purpose of this interrogation is denial: that is, they have not taken gods able to give life. "Am" here is the disjunctive "am," and the hamza is for denying occurrence. Al-Mubarrad said: "am" here has the meaning of "hal" (is it that): that is, have these polytheists taken gods from the earth who give life to the dead? "Am" here cannot mean "bal" (rather), because that would imply that they can create the dead, unless "am" is taken as accompanied by an interrogative, making it the disjunctive "am," and then the meaning is sound. "Min al-ard" (from the earth) is connected to "ittakhadhu" (took), or to an omitted word which is a description of "gods." The meaning of "they raise" is they resurrect the dead. The clause is a description of "gods." This clause is what the denial and ignorance-attribution revolve around, not the taking itself, since that takes place from them without doubt. The meaning: "Rather, they have taken gods from the earth, [gods] who alone, despite their lowliness, raise the dead." But that is not the case, for those they took as gods are far from that. Al-Jumhur read "yunshirun" with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the shin, from "anshara-hu," meaning "ahyahu" (gave him life). Al-Hasan read it with a fathah on the ya': that is, "yahyawna wa-la yamutun" (they live and do not die).

Then He, glorified is He, established proof of the invalidity of multiple gods, saying: ﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾: that is, had there been in the heavens and the earth gods worshipped other than Allah, they would have been ruined, meaning they would have been corrupted, namely the heavens and the earth with what is in them of creatures. Al-Kisa'i, Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and the majority of grammarians said: "illa" here is not for exception but means "ghayr" (other than), a description of "gods." That is why the noun after it was in the nominative and the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of "ghayr" appeared in it, since "illa" here has the meaning of "ghayr." From it is the saying of the poet:

And every brother whose brother departs from him, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads [i.e., they do not depart].

Al-Farra' said: "illa" here means "siwa" (other than): the meaning being: had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined. The reason for ruin is that the existence of another god with Allah necessitates that each of them be capable of independent control of management, so conflict and disagreement occur, and corruption is caused by it. End.

﴿So glorified is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾. The "fa" (so) is to order what follows upon what precedes, from the establishment of oneness by proof: that is, He is exalted, mighty and majestic, above what is not befitting for Him, such as the existence of a partner for Him. In this is guidance for the servants to declare the Lord, glorified is He, free of what is not befitting for Him.

﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾. This sentence is a new sentence explaining that He, glorified is He, because of the strength of His authority and the greatness of His majesty, is not asked by any of His creatures about any of His decree and destiny. ﴿But they will be questioned﴾, that is, the servants will be questioned about what they do; Allah will question them about that because they are His servants. It was also said: the meaning is that He, glorified is He, is not held accountable for His actions, while they are held accountable. It was said: the intended meaning is that He, glorified is He, made clear to His servants that whoever is questioned about his deeds, like the Messiah and the angels, is not suitable to be a god.

(p-933) ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ That is, "Rather, they have taken," and this is a shift (*idrab*) and a move from demonstrating the falsehood of their being gods by the preceding proof to demonstrating the falsehood of taking them as gods, while rebuking them by demanding proof from them. For this reason He said, ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ for the claim that they are gods, or for the permissibility of taking gods other than God. They have no way to any such thing, neither through reason (*'aql*) nor through transmitted evidence (*naql*). The proof of reason has already been explained, and as for the proof of transmission, He indicated it in His saying: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾. That is: this revelation concerning monotheism, which contains the decisive proof, is the reminder of my community and the reminder of the earlier nations. I have established it against you and made it clear to you, so you establish your proof. It was also said that the meaning is: this Qur'an and these earlier books that were sent down before me. Look and see whether in any one of them God commanded taking any god besides Him. Al-Zajjaj said: they were told, "Bring your proof that some messenger among the messengers informed his community that they have a god other than God. Is the mention of those with me and those before me anything but the oneness of God?" It was also said that the meaning of the speech is warning and threat, that is: do whatever you wish, for soon the veil will be lifted.

Abu Hatim related that Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "هذا ذكرٌ من معي وذكرٌ من قبلي" with tanwin on both *dhikr* words and with a kasra on the *mim* of *min*, and he claimed that there is no basis for this reading. Al-Zajjaj, in explaining this reading, said that the meaning is: "This is a reminder of what has been revealed to me and what is with me, and the reminder of those before me." It was also said: a reminder existing from before me, that is, I have brought what the prophets before me brought.

Then, when the proof was directed at them, He censured them for their ignorance of the places of truth, saying: ﴿Rather, most of them do not know the truth﴾. This is a shift (*idrab*) on His part, glorified is He, and a move from reproaching them by demanding proof to explaining that the establishment of proof does not affect them, because they are ignorant of the truth and cannot distinguish it from falsehood. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Hasan read *al-haqq* with a *damma* (as *al-haqqu*), in the sense of "this is the truth," or "it is the truth." The clause ﴿so they are turning away﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, namely that most of them do not know. That is: because of this ignorance that prevails over most of them, they are turning away from accepting the truth, persisting in turning away from monotheism and from following the Messenger. Therefore they do not consider any argument, nor reflect on any proof, nor ponder any evidence.

﴿We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me.﴾ Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *nuhi* with the *nun*, while the rest read it with the *ya'*, that is, "We reveal to him." And in this is an affirmation of the matter of monotheism and an emphasis on what came earlier in His saying: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾. He concluded the verse with the command to His servants to worship Him, saying ﴿so worship Me﴾. Thus the proof of reason and the proof of transmission have become clear to you, and God's proof has been established against you.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your mention﴾, that he said: "Your honor." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: "In it is your news." In another report from him he said: "In it is your religion."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, through the route of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "God sent a prophet from Himyar called Shu'ayb. A servant (of the king) leapt at him and struck him with a staff. Bukhtanassar then marched against them, fought them, and killed them until none of them remained. And concerning them God revealed ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ to His saying ﴿extinguished﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Kalbi regarding His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ that he said: "It is the town of Hadur, of the Azd." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿and return to that in which you were given luxury﴾ that he said: "Return to your homes and your wealth."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿and that claim of theirs did not cease﴾ that he said: "They are the people of Hadur who had killed their prophet, so God sent Bukhtanassar against them and he killed them." And regarding His saying ﴿We made them as harvested crops, extinguished﴾ he said: "With the sword; the angels struck their faces until they returned to their dwellings."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Wahb, who said: "A man from the people of al-Jazar related to me: Yemen was two towns, one called Hadur and the other Qilabah. They became insolent and were given luxury, until they did not even close their doors. When they had been given luxury, God sent them a prophet who called them, but they killed him. So God put into the heart of Bukhtanassar that he should attack them, and he equipped an army for them. They fought them, and they defeated his army, so they returned to him in defeat. He then equipped against them a second army, larger than the first, and they defeated them too. When Bukhtanassar saw this, he went out to fight them himself, and they fought him, and he defeated them until they fled out of the town running. They heard a caller calling, ﴿Do not run, but return to that in which you were given luxury and to your dwellings﴾, so they returned. Then they heard a voice calling, 'O vengeance for the Prophet!' and they were killed by the sword. This is what God referred to in His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ to His saying 'extinguished'."

I say: The villages of Hadur are well known today, between them and the city of Sana'a, about one *barid* (a unit of distance) to the west of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿harvested crops, extinguished﴾ that he said: "Like the extinguishing of fire when it is put out." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ that he said: "The pastime is a child." Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ that he said: "The women." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and they do not tire﴾ that he said: "They do not return." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ that he said: "about His servants," ﴿but they will be questioned﴾, he said: "about their deeds." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded a similar report from al-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is no people on earth more hateful to me than the Qadariyyah (a sect that denied divine predestination), and that is only because they do not know the power of God." God says, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 26–35:**

.

His words: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ These sayers were the tribe of Khuza'a, for they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." It was also said that they were the Jews, and the verse can be applied to everyone who ascribes a son to Allah. The Jews said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and a group of the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, declared Himself free of this, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning, a declaration of His transcendence above that, and it is an expression uttered by the tongues of His servants. Then He turned away from their statement and refuted it, saying: ﴿Nay, they are honoured servants﴾, meaning, they are not as they claimed, but rather they are servants of Allah, Glorified be He, honoured by His favour toward them, and brought near to Him. It has been read as ﴿mukarramun﴾ with the doubled letter (shadda). Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' permitted the accusative reading of ﴿'ibadan﴾ (servants) with the meaning: "Rather, He has taken servants." Then He described them with another attribute, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning, they do not say anything until He has said it, or has commanded them to say it. Thus said Ibn Qutayba and others. In this there is evidence of the perfection of their obedience and submission. It has been read as ﴿la yasbuqunahu﴾ with a damma on the ba' (yasbuqunahu), from sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu. ﴿And they act by His command﴾, meaning, they are the ones who act according to what Allah commands them, following Him and obeying their Lord. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it. That is, He knows what they have done and what they are doing. Or, He knows what is before them, which is the Hereafter, and what is behind them, which is this world. The reasoning behind the justification is that when they know that He knows what they have advanced and what they have left behind, they will not do any deed or say any word except by His command. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning, the intercessors intercede for him, and he is the one with whom He is pleased. It was also said that they are the people of "There is no god but Allah." It is established in the Sahih that the angels will intercede in the Hereafter. ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning, out of their fear of Him. The verbal noun is thus annexed to its object, and khashya is fear arising from reverence, while ishfaq is fear arising from anticipation and caution, that is, they do not feel safe from the plan of Allah.

﴿And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him"﴾, meaning, whoever among the angels says, "I am a god besides Allah." The commentators said: by this is meant Iblis, for none of the angels said, "I am a god," except Iblis. It was also said that the reference is to all the prophets. ﴿That is how We recompense him: Hell﴾, meaning, that sayer, on the assumption and supposition, We recompense him with Hell because of this statement he uttered, just as We recompense others among the criminals. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, meaning, with a recompense like that terrible one We recompense the wrongdoers; or, like what We made the recompense of this sayer, Hell, so likewise We recompense the wrongdoers who place divinity and worship where they do not belong. By "the wrongdoers" are meant the polytheists.

﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen﴾: the hamza is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause. The seeing here is intellectual, meaning: Have they not reflected, or do they not know, ﴿that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass﴾. Al-Akhfash said: He said "kanata" (were, dual) because they are two kinds, that is, the collective of the heavens and the earths, as He, Glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "kanata" because He refers to the heavens with the singular form, since the heavens were one heaven, and likewise the earths. Ratq means a closure, the opposite of fatq (splitting). It is said: "I closed the split (rataqtu al-fatq), I close it, and it closed up (irtataqa)," meaning, it became joined. From this comes "al-ratqa'," for a woman whose vagina is closed. The meaning is that the two were one thing, stuck together, and Allah separated them. He said ratqan and not ratqayn because it is a verbal noun. The implied sense is: they were possessors of closure. The meaning of ﴿then We parted them﴾ is that We separated them: that is, We separated some of them from others, so We raised the sky and left the earth in its place. ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾, meaning, by the water that We send down from the sky We gave life to every living thing, so this includes animals and plants. The meaning is that water is the cause of the life of everything. It was also said that the water here means the sperm-drop (nutfa), and most of the commentators held this view. This is an argument against the polytheists based on the power of Allah, Glorified be He, and His wondrous creation. The explanation of this verse has already been given before. The hamza in ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ is for denunciation of them, since they did not believe despite the presence of the divine signs that call for belief.

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, meaning, firm mountains. ﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾: al-maid is movement and turning, meaning, lest it move and turn with them, or out of aversion to that. The explanation of this has already been given in full in al-Nahl. ﴿And We made in it﴾, meaning, in the mountains, or in the earth, ﴿broad passages﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: these are paths. Al-Zajjaj said: every opening between two mountains is a fajj, and ﴿paths﴾ is an explanation of the fijaj, because a fajj may not be a passable, traveled road. ﴿That they may be guided﴾ to the benefits of their livelihood and what their needs call for.

﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾, protected from falling and collapsing onto the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth﴾ [al-Hajj: 65]. Al-Farra' said: "protected" by the stars from the devil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ [al-Hijr: 17]. It was also said: protected, needing no pillars. It was also said: the meaning of "protected" here is "raised." It was also said: protected from polytheism and sins. It was also said: protected from demolition and breaking. ﴿Yet they turn away from its signs﴾. He attributed the signs to the sky because they are placed in it, such as the sun, the moon, and the like. The meaning of turning away is that they do not contemplate them, and do not reflect on what they require of faith.

﴿And it is He who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾. This is a reminder to them of another blessing among those with which He has favoured them: He created the night for them to rest in it, and the day for them to move about in their livelihoods. He created the sun and the moon, that is, He made the sun a sign of the day and the moon a sign of the night, so that they might know the number of months and the reckoning, as its explanation has already been given in Subhan. ﴿Each in an orbit they swim﴾, meaning, each one of the sun, the moon, and the stars swims in an orbit: that is, they move in the middle of the orbit and travel swiftly like a swimmer in water. The plural in the verb is in view of the risings. Sibawayh said: when He reported about them with the verb of rational beings, and made them in obedience like rational beings, He made the pronoun for them the pronoun of rational beings, and did not say yasbahna or tasbahu. Al-Farra' said likewise. Al-Kisa'i said: He only said yasbahun because it is the end of a verse. The falak is the orbit of the stars, and the root of the word is from rotation, and from it comes "falaka al-mighzal" (the spindle whorl), because of its roundness.

﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, meaning, lasting permanence in this world. ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾, meaning, will they then be the immortal ones? Al-Farra' said: He used the fa' to indicate the condition, since it is the answer to their saying, "He will die." He said: it is permissible to omit the fa' and to leave it implied, and the meaning is: if you die, they will also die, so there is no gloating at death. ﴿Mitta﴾ has been read with a kasra and a damma on the mim, both being dialectal forms. The cause of the revelation of this verse was the statement of the polytheists, as Allah reported about them: ﴿Or do they say, "He is a poet; we await for him the misfortunes of time"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30].

Then He described them with another attribute, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning, they do not say anything until He has said it, or has commanded them to say it. It has been read as ﴿la yasbuqunahu﴾ with a damma on the ba' (yasbuqunahu), from sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu. ﴿And they act by His command﴾, meaning, they are the ones who act according to what Allah commands them, following Him and obeying their Lord. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it. That is, He knows what they have done and what they are doing. Or, He knows what is before them, which is the Hereafter, and what is behind them, which is this world. The reasoning behind the justification is that when they know that He knows what they have advanced and what they have left behind, they will not do any deed or say any word except by His command. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning, the intercessors intercede for him, and he is the one with whom He is pleased. It was also said that they are the people of "There is no god but Allah." It is established in the Sahih that the angels will intercede in the Hereafter. ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning, out of their fear of Him. The verbal noun is thus annexed to its object, and khashya is fear arising from reverence, while ishfaq is fear arising from anticipation and caution, that is, they do not feel safe from the plan of Allah.

The commentators said: by this is meant Iblis, for none of the angels said, "I am a god," except Iblis. Al-Akhfash said: He said "kanata" (were, dual) because they are two kinds, that is, the collective of the heavens and the earths, as He, Glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. He said ratqan and not ratqayn because it is a verbal noun. The implied sense is: they were possessors of closure. **Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 26–35:**

.

His words: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ These sayers were the tribe of Khuza'a, for they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." It was also said that they were the Jews, and the verse can be applied to everyone who ascribes a son to Allah. The Jews said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and a group of the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, declared Himself free of this, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning, a declaration of His transcendence above that, and it is an expression uttered by the tongues of His servants. Then He turned away from their statement and refuted it, saying: ﴿Nay, they are honoured servants﴾, meaning, they are not as they claimed, but rather they are servants of Allah, Glorified be He, honoured by His favour toward them, and brought near to Him. It has been read as ﴿mukarramun﴾ with the doubled letter (shadda). Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' permitted the accusative reading of ﴿'ibadan﴾ (servants) with the meaning: "Rather, He has taken servants." Then He described them with another attribute, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning, they do not say anything until He has said it, or has commanded them to say it. Thus said Ibn Qutayba and others. In this there is evidence of the perfection of their obedience and submission. It has been read as ﴿la yasbuqunahu﴾ with a damma on the ba' (yasbuqunahu), from sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu. ﴿And they act by His command﴾, meaning, they are the ones who act according to what Allah commands them, following Him and obeying their Lord. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it. That is, He knows what they have done and what they are doing. Or, He knows what is before them, which is the Hereafter, and what is behind them, which is this world. The reasoning behind the justification is that when they know that He knows what they have advanced and what they have left behind, they will not do any deed or say any word except by His command. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning, the intercessors intercede for him, and he is the one with whom He is pleased. It was also said that they are the people of "There is no god but Allah." It is established in the Sahih that the angels will intercede in the Hereafter. ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning, out of their fear of Him. The verbal noun is thus annexed to its object, and khashya is fear arising from reverence, while ishfaq is fear arising from anticipation and caution, that is, they do not feel safe from the plan of Allah.

﴿And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him"﴾, meaning, whoever among the angels says, "I am a god besides Allah." The commentators said: by this is meant Iblis, for none of the angels said, "I am a god," except Iblis. It was also said that the reference is to all the prophets. ﴿That is how We recompense him: Hell﴾, meaning, that sayer, on the assumption and supposition, We recompense him with Hell because of this statement he uttered, just as We recompense others among the criminals. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, meaning, with a recompense like that terrible one We recompense the wrongdoers; or, like what We made the recompense of this sayer, Hell, so likewise We recompense the wrongdoers who place divinity and worship where they do not belong. By "the wrongdoers" are meant the polytheists.

﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen﴾: the hamza is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause. The seeing here is intellectual, meaning: Have they not reflected, or do they not know, ﴿that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass﴾. Al-Akhfash said: He said "kanata" (were, dual) because they are two kinds, that is, the collective of the heavens and the earths, as He, Glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "kanata" because He refers to the heavens with the singular form, since the heavens were one heaven, and likewise the earths. Ratq means a closure, the opposite of fatq (splitting). It is said: "I closed the split (rataqtu al-fatq), I close it, and it closed up (irtataqa)," meaning, it became joined. From this comes "al-ratqa'," for a woman whose vagina is closed. The meaning is that the two were one thing, stuck together, and Allah separated them. He said ratqan and not ratqayn because it is a verbal noun. The implied sense is: they were possessors of closure. The meaning of ﴿then We parted them﴾ is that We separated them: that is, We separated some of them from others, so We raised the sky and left the earth in its place. ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾, meaning, by the water that We send down from the sky We gave life to every living thing, so this includes animals and plants. The meaning is that water is the cause of the life of everything. It was also said that the water here means the sperm-drop (nutfa), and most of the commentators held this view. This is an argument against the polytheists based on the power of Allah, Glorified be He, and His wondrous creation. The explanation of this verse has already been given before. The hamza in ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ is for denunciation of them, since they did not believe despite the presence of the divine signs that call for belief.

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, meaning, firm mountains. ﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾: al-maid is movement and turning, meaning, lest it move and turn with them, or out of aversion to that. The explanation of this has already been given in full in al-Nahl. ﴿And We made in it﴾, meaning, in the mountains, or in the earth, ﴿broad passages﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: these are paths. Al-Zajjaj said: every opening between two mountains is a fajj, and ﴿paths﴾ is an explanation of the fijaj, because a fajj may not be a passable, traveled road. ﴿That they may be guided﴾ to the benefits of their livelihood and what their needs call for.

﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾, protected from falling and collapsing onto the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth﴾ [al-Hajj: 65]. Al-Farra' said: "protected" by the stars from the devil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ [al-Hijr: 17]. It was also said: protected, needing no pillars. It was also said: the meaning of "protected" here is "raised." It was also said: protected from polytheism and sins. He attributed the signs to the sky because they are placed in it, such as the sun, the moon, and the like. The meaning of turning away is that they do not contemplate them, and do not reflect on what they require of faith.

The plural in the verb is in view of the risings. Al-Farra' said likewise. Al-Kisa'i said: He only said yasbahun because it is the end of a verse. The falak is the orbit of the stars, and the root of the word is from rotation, and from it comes "falaka al-mighzal" (the spindle whorl), because of its roundness.

The cause of the revelation of this verse was the statement of the polytheists, as Allah reported about them: ﴿Or do they say, "He is a poet; we await for him the misfortunes of time"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30].

﴿Every soul will taste death﴾, meaning, it will be one tasting the separation from its body, so no one among the created souls will remain, whatever he may be. ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾, meaning, We test you with hardship and ease, so that We may see how you are grateful and how you are patient. His words: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ These sayers were the tribe of Khuza'a, for they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Then He described them with another attribute, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning, they do not say anything until He has said it, or has commanded them to say it. It has been read as ﴿la yasbuqunahu﴾ with a damma on the ba' (yasbuqunahu), from sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu. ﴿And they act by His command﴾, meaning, they are the ones who act according to what Allah commands them, following Him and obeying their Lord. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it. That is, He knows what they have done and what they are doing. Or, He knows what is before them, which is the Hereafter, and what is behind them, which is this world. The reasoning behind the justification is that when they know that He knows what they have advanced and what they have left behind, they will not do any deed or say any word except by His command. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning, the intercessors intercede for him, and he is the one with whom He is pleased. It was also said that they are the people of "There is no god but Allah." It is established in the Sahih that the angels will intercede in the Hereafter. ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning, out of their fear of Him. The verbal noun is thus annexed to its object, and khashya is fear arising from reverence, while ishfaq is fear arising from anticipation and caution, that is, they do not feel safe from the plan of Allah.

﴿And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him"﴾, meaning, whoever among the angels says, "I am a god besides Allah." The commentators said: by this is meant Iblis, for none of the angels said, "I am a god," except Iblis. It was also said that the reference is to all the prophets. ﴿That is how We recompense him: Hell﴾, meaning, that sayer, on the assumption and supposition, We recompense him with Hell because of this statement he uttered, just as We recompense others among the criminals. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, meaning, with a recompense like that terrible one We recompense the wrongdoers; or, like what We made the recompense of this sayer, Hell, so likewise We recompense the wrongdoers who place divinity and worship where they do not belong. ﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen﴾: the hamza is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause. The seeing here is intellectual, meaning: Have they not reflected, or do they not know, ﴿that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass﴾. Al-Akhfash said: He said "kanata" (were, dual) because they are two kinds, that is, the collective of the heavens and the earths, as He, Glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "kanata" because He refers to the heavens with the singular form, since the heavens were one heaven, and likewise the earths. From this comes "al-ratqa'," for a woman whose vagina is closed. The meaning is that the two were one thing, stuck together, and Allah separated them. He said ratqan and not ratqayn because it is a verbal noun. The implied sense is: they were possessors of closure. This is an argument against the polytheists based on the power of Allah, Glorified be He, and His wondrous creation. The explanation of this verse has already been given before. Al-Farra' said likewise. Al-Kisa'i said: He only said yasbahun because it is the end of a verse.
