Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from 'A'isha: Abu Bakr entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) when he had died, and he kissed him and said: "O Prophet! O friend! O chosen one!" Then he recited: ﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, the verse, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30]. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾, he said: We test you with hardship and ease, health and sickness, wealth and poverty, the lawful and the unlawful, obedience and disobedience, guidance and misguidance.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 26–35:**

.

His words: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ These sayers were the tribe of Khuza'a, for they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." It was also said that they were the Jews, and the verse can be applied to everyone who ascribes a son to Allah. The Jews said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and a group of the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, declared Himself free of this, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning, a declaration of His transcendence above that, and it is an expression uttered by the tongues of His servants. Then He turned away from their statement and refuted it, saying: ﴿Nay, they are honoured servants﴾, meaning, they are not as they claimed, but rather they are servants of Allah, Glorified be He, honoured by His favour toward them, and brought near to Him. It has been read as ﴿mukarramun﴾ with the doubled letter (shadda). Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' permitted the accusative reading of ﴿'ibadan﴾ (servants) with the meaning: "Rather, He has taken servants." Then He described them with another attribute, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning, they do not say anything until He has said it, or has commanded them to say it. Thus said Ibn Qutayba and others. In this there is evidence of the perfection of their obedience and submission. It has been read as ﴿la yasbuqunahu﴾ with a damma on the ba' (yasbuqunahu), from sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu. ﴿And they act by His command﴾, meaning, they are the ones who act according to what Allah commands them, following Him and obeying their Lord. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it. That is, He knows what they have done and what they are doing. Or, He knows what is before them, which is the Hereafter, and what is behind them, which is this world. The reasoning behind the justification is that when they know that He knows what they have advanced and what they have left behind, they will not do any deed or say any word except by His command. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning, the intercessors intercede for him, and he is the one with whom He is pleased. It was also said that they are the people of "There is no god but Allah." It is established in the Sahih that the angels will intercede in the Hereafter. ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning, out of their fear of Him. The verbal noun is thus annexed to its object, and khashya is fear arising from reverence, while ishfaq is fear arising from anticipation and caution, that is, they do not feel safe from the plan of Allah.

﴿And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him"﴾, meaning, whoever among the angels says, "I am a god besides Allah." The commentators said: by this is meant Iblis, for none of the angels said, "I am a god," except Iblis. It was also said that the reference is to all the prophets. ﴿That is how We recompense him: Hell﴾, meaning, that sayer, on the assumption and supposition, We recompense him with Hell because of this statement he uttered, just as We recompense others among the criminals. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, meaning, with a recompense like that terrible one We recompense the wrongdoers; or, like what We made the recompense of this sayer, Hell, so likewise We recompense the wrongdoers who place divinity and worship where they do not belong. By "the wrongdoers" are meant the polytheists.

﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen﴾: the hamza is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause. The seeing here is intellectual, meaning: Have they not reflected, or do they not know, ﴿that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass﴾. Al-Akhfash said: He said "kanata" (were, dual) because they are two kinds, that is, the collective of the heavens and the earths, as He, Glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "kanata" because He refers to the heavens with the singular form, since the heavens were one heaven, and likewise the earths. Ratq means a closure, the opposite of fatq (splitting). It is said: "I closed the split (rataqtu al-fatq), I close it, and it closed up (irtataqa)," meaning, it became joined. From this comes "al-ratqa'," for a woman whose vagina is closed. The meaning is that the two were one thing, stuck together, and Allah separated them. He said ratqan and not ratqayn because it is a verbal noun. The implied sense is: they were possessors of closure. The meaning of ﴿then We parted them﴾ is that We separated them: that is, We separated some of them from others, so We raised the sky and left the earth in its place. ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾, meaning, by the water that We send down from the sky We gave life to every living thing, so this includes animals and plants. The meaning is that water is the cause of the life of everything. It was also said that the water here means the sperm-drop (nutfa), and most of the commentators held this view. This is an argument against the polytheists based on the power of Allah, Glorified be He, and His wondrous creation. The explanation of this verse has already been given before. The hamza in ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ is for denunciation of them, since they did not believe despite the presence of the divine signs that call for belief.

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, meaning, firm mountains. ﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾: al-maid is movement and turning, meaning, lest it move and turn with them, or out of aversion to that. The explanation of this has already been given in full in al-Nahl. ﴿And We made in it﴾, meaning, in the mountains, or in the earth, ﴿broad passages﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: these are paths. Al-Zajjaj said: every opening between two mountains is a fajj, and ﴿paths﴾ is an explanation of the fijaj, because a fajj may not be a passable, traveled road. ﴿That they may be guided﴾ to the benefits of their livelihood and what their needs call for.

﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾, protected from falling and collapsing onto the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth﴾ [al-Hajj: 65]. Al-Farra' said: "protected" by the stars from the devil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ [al-Hijr: 17]. It was also said: protected, needing no pillars. It was also said: the meaning of "protected" here is "raised." It was also said: protected from polytheism and sins. It was also said: protected from demolition and breaking. ﴿Yet they turn away from its signs﴾. He attributed the signs to the sky because they are placed in it, such as the sun, the moon, and the like. The meaning of turning away is that they do not contemplate them, and do not reflect on what they require of faith.

﴿And it is He who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾. This is a reminder to them of another blessing among those with which He has favoured them: He created the night for them to rest in it, and the day for them to move about in their livelihoods. He created the sun and the moon, that is, He made the sun a sign of the day and the moon a sign of the night, so that they might know the number of months and the reckoning, as its explanation has already been given in Subhan. ﴿Each in an orbit they swim﴾, meaning, each one of the sun, the moon, and the stars swims in an orbit: that is, they move in the middle of the orbit and travel swiftly like a swimmer in water. The plural in the verb is in view of the risings. Sibawayh said: when He reported about them with the verb of rational beings, and made them in obedience like rational beings, He made the pronoun for them the pronoun of rational beings, and did not say yasbahna or tasbahu. Al-Farra' said likewise. Al-Kisa'i said: He only said yasbahun because it is the end of a verse. The falak is the orbit of the stars, and the root of the word is from rotation, and from it comes "falaka al-mighzal" (the spindle whorl), because of its roundness.

﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, meaning, lasting permanence in this world. ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾, meaning, will they then be the immortal ones? Al-Farra' said: He used the fa' to indicate the condition, since it is the answer to their saying, "He will die." He said: it is permissible to omit the fa' and to leave it implied, and the meaning is: if you die, they will also die, so there is no gloating at death. ﴿Mitta﴾ has been read with a kasra and a damma on the mim, both being dialectal forms. The cause of the revelation of this verse was the statement of the polytheists, as Allah reported about them: ﴿Or do they say, "He is a poet; we await for him the misfortunes of time"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30].

﴿Every soul will taste death﴾, meaning, it will be one tasting the separation from its body, so no one among the created souls will remain, whatever he may be. ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾, meaning, We test you with hardship and ease, so that We may see how you are grateful and how you are patient. The meaning is that He, Glorified be He, treats them as one who tests them. Fitna is a verbal noun for ﴿nabluwakum﴾ (We test you), not from its own root. ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾, not to other than Us, so We will repay you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, who said: The Jews said, "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, became related by marriage to the jinn, and the angels were their offspring." So Allah said, refuting them: ﴿Nay, they are honoured servants﴾, meaning, the angels are not as they claimed, but rather they are servants whom He honoured with His worship. ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ (p. 935) ﴿He praises them﴾. He said: ﴿And they do not intercede﴾, he said: The angels will not intercede on the Day of Resurrection ﴿except for one whom He approves﴾; he said: for the people of monotheism. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿except for one whom He approves﴾: for the people of monotheism, for whom He is pleased. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from al-Hasan concerning the verse: the statement "There is no god but Allah." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse: those whom He approved for the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th reported from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, and said: "My intercession is for the people of major sins from my community." Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿That the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, then We parted them﴾, he said: The sky was split by the rain, and the earth was split by vegetation. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning ﴿a joined mass﴾, he said: nothing comes out of the two, and he mentioned the same as what preceded. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya also reported it from him through another route. Ibn Jarir reported from him concerning ﴿a joined mass﴾: stuck together. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Abu al-'Aliya concerning His saying: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾, he said: the sperm-drop of a man. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And We made in it broad passages as roads﴾, he said: between the mountains. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Each in an orbit﴾, he said: a rotation; ﴿they swim﴾, he said: they run. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama reported from him: ﴿Each in an orbit﴾, he said: an orbit like the whorl of a spindle; ﴿they swim﴾, he said: they revolve in the gates of the sky as the whorl revolves on the spindle. Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him: he said: it is the orbit of the sky. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from 'A'isha: Abu Bakr entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) when he had died, and he kissed him and said: "O Prophet! O friend! O chosen one!" Then he recited: ﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, the verse, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30]. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾, he said: We test you with hardship and ease, health and sickness, wealth and poverty, the lawful and the unlawful, obedience and disobedience, guidance and misguidance.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 36–43**

His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieve see you﴾, meaning the mockers among the polytheists, ﴿they take you not except in mockery﴾. That is, they take you only as an object of ridicule. Al-hazw (mockery) is ridicule. These are the ones about whom God said: ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 95]. The meaning is: they do nothing to you except take you as a target of mockery. ﴿"Is this the one who mentions your gods?"﴾ is in the sense of an implied "they say": that is, they say, "Is this the one who…" So on this reading it is the answer to "when" (idha), and his saying ﴿they take you not except in mockery﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the condition and its answer. The meaning of "mentions them" (yadhkuruha) is "disparages them."

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "So-and-so mentions people" (yadhkuru al-nas), meaning he backbites them and mentions their faults. And "So-and-so mentions God" (yadhkuru Allah) means he describes Him with glorification and praises Him. The word is omitted together with "mention" only when its meaning is understood. According to what they have said, "mention" in the speech of the Arabs does not mean "fault." Where "fault" is intended, the word "evil" (al-su') is dropped from it. It is said that this includes the verse of ʿAntara:

*Do not mention my colt, or what I have fed him, lest your skin become like the skin of a mangy camel.*

That is, do not disparage my colt.

His saying: ﴿and they, in the remembrance of the Most Merciful, are disbelievers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) in the accusative. That is: while they are disbelievers in the Qur'an, or they are disbelievers in the remembrance of the Most Merciful who created them. The meaning is: they find fault with the Prophet (ﷺ) for mentioning their gods, which neither harm nor benefit, with evil, while the actual situation is that they disbelieve in the remembrance of God, glorified is He, in a manner befitting Him, of monotheism, or of the Qur'an. So they are more deserving of blame and of rebuke than he. The first pronoun is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is "disbelievers," and "in the remembrance" is connected to the predicate. The second pronoun is for emphasis.

﴿Man was created from haste﴾: that is, he was made, because of his excessive hastiness, as if he were created from haste. Al-Farra' said: It is as if he says, "I built him and created him from haste and upon haste." Al-Zajjaj said: The Arabs were addressed in terms they understand, and the Arabs say of one who does a thing excessively, "You were created from it," just as they say, "You are made of play" (anta min la'ib) and "You were created from play," intending hyperbole in describing him with that. What indicates this meaning is His saying: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾ [al-Isra': 11]. "Man" here refers to the species. It is also said that "man" refers to Adam. When God created him and breathed the spirit into him, the spirit reached his head, so he tried to rise before the spirit reached his feet, and he fell. So it was said: ﴿Man was created from haste.﴾ Thus said ʿIkrima, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi, and Mujahid. Abu ʿUbayda and many of the scholars of meanings said: "ʿajal" means clay in the dialect of Himyar.

They recited:

*And the palm grows between the water and the ʿajal.*

It is also said that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who is the one who said: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. And it is said it was revealed concerning Quraysh, because they sought the punishment hastily.

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning of ﴿Man was created from haste﴾ is that it was said to him, "Be," and he was.

It is also said that this verse is of the inverted type (al-maqlub): that is, haste was created from man. This has been reported from Abu ʿUbayda and al-Nahhas, but the first view is preferable. (p-936)

﴿I will show you My signs﴾: that is, I will show you My vengeance upon you through the punishment of the Fire. ﴿So do not hasten Me﴾: that is, do not hasten Me to bring it, for it will certainly descend upon you. It is said that the "signs" refers to what indicates the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) from the miracles and what God made for him of the praiseworthy outcome. The first view is preferable.

This is indicated by their saying: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ That is: when will this promise be fulfilled, the punishment you promise us? They said this by way of mockery and derision. It is also said that "the promise" here means the Resurrection. The meaning of ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is: if you, O company of Muslims, are truthful in your promise. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers who recite the Qur'anic verses warning of the coming of the Hour and the imminence of the punishment.

The clause ﴿If only those who disbelieve would know﴾ and what follows it confirms what precedes it. That is: if they knew that time. The answer to "if only" (law) is omitted, and the implied meaning is: if they knew the time ﴿when they will not withhold the Fire from their faces or from their backs, nor will they be helped﴾, they would not have hastened the threat.

Al-Zajjaj said: In estimating the answer, [it is]: so that they would know the truth of the promise. It is also said: if they knew it, they would not persist in disbelief. Al-Kisa'i said: It is a warning to establish the certainty of the occurrence of the Hour: that is, if they knew it with certain knowledge, they would know that the Hour is coming. What indicates this is His saying: ﴿But it will come upon them suddenly﴾. The specification of "faces" and "backs" by mention, in the sense of front and rear, is because they are the most prominent sides, and encompassing them entails encompassing everything, so that they cannot repel it from any of their sides. The position of "when" (hina) in "when they will not withhold" is accusative, as it is the object of "know." It refers to the appointed time they used to seek hastily. The meaning of ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ is: no one among the servants will help them, so as to repel that from them.

The clause ﴿But it will come upon them suddenly﴾ is conjoined to "they will withhold": that is, they will not withhold it, but the promise, or the Fire, or the Hour, will come upon them suddenly: that is, unexpectedly, so it will confound them. Al-Jawhari said: "bahatahu" means he took him by surprise. Al-Farra' said: "fa-tabhutuhum" means it will bewilder them. It is also said: it will startle them. ﴿So they will not be able to repel it﴾: that is, to turn it away from their faces or from their backs. The pronoun refers to the Fire. It is also said that it refers to the promise, by interpreting it as the "appointed time," and it is also said that it refers to "the time," by interpreting it as the Hour. ﴿Nor will they be granted respite﴾: that is, they will not be given time or deferred for repentance or excuse.

The clause ﴿And certainly were mocked messengers before you﴾ is brought to console and comfort the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is as if He said: If these have mocked you, then it has been done to the messengers before you, despite their great number and the significance of their station. ﴿So there descended upon those who ridiculed them﴾: that is, there encompassed and turned upon them because of that, upon those who ridiculed and mocked those messengers, ﴿what they used to mock.﴾ The "what" (ma) is a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a verbal particle (masdariyya). That is: there encompassed them the matter at which they used to mock, or there encompassed them their mockery, that is, its recompense, by putting the cause in place of the effect, or the mockery itself, if by it is meant the otherworldly punishment.

﴿Say: "Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?"﴾: that is, who guards and preserves you. Al-kala'a is guarding and preservation. It is said: "kalaahu Allah kilaa'atan" with a kasra, meaning God preserved him and guarded him.

Ibn Harma said:

*Indeed Sulayma, and God protects her, is stingy with a thing that would not diminish her.*

That is: say, O Muhammad, to those mockers, by way of reproach and rebuke: who guards and protects you by night and day from the might of the Most Merciful and His punishment, which you deserve to befall you and descend upon you? Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "who protects you from the might of the Most Merciful?"

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is, "who protects you from what the Most Merciful wills to bring down upon you of the punishments of this world and the Hereafter?" Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related: "man yaklu'kum" with a fatha on the lam and a sukun on the waw. ﴿Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾: that is, from the remembrance of Him, glorified is He, so they do not mention Him and do not bring Him to mind, but turn away from Him, or from the Qur'an, or from the admonitions of God, or from knowing Him.

﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from beside Us?﴾ The "am" here is the disjunctive one, which means "rather" (bal). The hamza is for transition and turning away from the previous speech, which contains a statement of their ignorance of His preserving them, to rebuking and reproaching them for relying on one who is incapable of benefiting himself or defending himself. The meaning is: rather, they have gods that protect them from Our punishment. It is also said there is inversion and displacement; the estimate is: "or do they have gods from beside Us that protect them?" Then He described these gods of theirs, whom they claimed would help them, with what indicates weakness and incapacity, saying: ﴿They are not able to help themselves, nor are they accompanied by Us﴾: that is, they are incapable of helping themselves, so how could they help others? "Nor are they accompanied by Us" means: nor are they given protection from Our punishment. Ibn Qutayba said: That is, no one gives them protection from Us, because the one who gives protection is "the companion of the protected," and the Arabs say, "God accompany you" (sahibaka Allah), meaning He guard you and grant you protection. From this is the poet's saying:

*He calls out with the top of his voice, seeking refuge, so that he may be protected from us, while the spears are reaching him.*

The Arabs say: "I am your protector and companion against so-and-so," meaning I grant protection from him. Al-Mazini said: It is from "asbahtu al-rajul," when you prevent him. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by Abu Sufyan and Abu Jahl while they were conversing. When Abu Jahl saw him he laughed and said to Abu Sufyan: 'This is the prophet of the Banu ʿAbd Manaf.' Abu Sufyan became angry and said: 'What do you find strange in that the Banu ʿAbd Manaf should have a prophet?' The Prophet (ﷺ) heard them, so he returned to Abu Jahl, rebuked him, and warned him, saying: 'I do not see you ceasing until there befalls you what befell your uncle.' And he said to Abu Sufyan: 'As for you, you did not say what you said except out of zealotry.' Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And when those who disbelieve see you﴾." I say: Look into who it was from whom al-Suddi related.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrima, who said: "When the spirit was breathed into Adam, it reached his head, so he sneezed and said, 'Praise be to God.' The angels said, 'May God have mercy on you.' Then he tried to rise before it reached his feet, so he fell. God said: ﴿Man was created from haste.﴾" Something similar was related by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Something similar was also related by Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzama from Mujahid. Likewise Ibn al-Mundhir related it from Ibn Jurayj.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿Say: "Who protects you?"﴾, that he said: "guards you." And concerning (p-937) His saying ﴿nor are they accompanied by Us﴾, he said: "They will not be helped." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿nor are they accompanied by Us﴾, that he said: "They will not be protected." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "They will not be prevented."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 36–43**

His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieve see you﴾, meaning the mockers among the polytheists, ﴿they take you not except in mockery﴾. That is, they take you only as an object of ridicule. Al-hazw (mockery) is ridicule. These are the ones about whom God said: ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 95]. The meaning is: they do nothing to you except take you as a target of mockery. ﴿"Is this the one who mentions your gods?"﴾ is in the sense of an implied "they say": that is, they say, "Is this the one who…" So on this reading it is the answer to "when" (idha), and his saying ﴿they take you not except in mockery﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the condition and its answer. The meaning of "mentions them" (yadhkuruha) is "disparages them."

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "So-and-so mentions people" (yadhkuru al-nas), meaning he backbites them and mentions their faults. And "So-and-so mentions God" (yadhkuru Allah) means he describes Him with glorification and praises Him. The word is omitted together with "mention" only when its meaning is understood. *Indeed Sulayma, and God protects her, is stingy with a thing that would not diminish her.*

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "So-and-so mentions people" (yadhkuru al-nas), meaning he backbites them and mentions their faults. From this is the poet's saying:

*He calls out with the top of his voice, seeking refuge, so that he may be protected from us, while the spears are reaching him.*

The Arabs say: "I am your protector and companion against so-and-so," meaning I grant protection from him. Al-Mazini said: It is from "asbahtu al-rajul," when you prevent him. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by Abu Sufyan and Abu Jahl while they were conversing. When Abu Jahl saw him he laughed and said to Abu Sufyan: 'This is the prophet of the Banu ʿAbd Manaf.' Abu Sufyan became angry and said: 'What do you find strange in that the Banu ʿAbd Manaf should have a prophet?' The Prophet (ﷺ) heard them, so he returned to Abu Jahl, rebuked him, and warned him, saying: 'I do not see you ceasing until there befalls you what befell your uncle.' And he said to Abu Sufyan: 'As for you, you did not say what you said except out of zealotry.' Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And when those who disbelieve see you﴾." I say: Look into who it was from whom al-Suddi related.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrima, who said: "When the spirit was breathed into Adam, it reached his head, so he sneezed and said, 'Praise be to God.' The angels said, 'May God have mercy on you.' Then he tried to rise before it reached his feet, so he fell. God said: ﴿Man was created from haste.﴾" Something similar was related by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Something similar was also related by Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzama from Mujahid. Likewise Ibn al-Mundhir related it from Ibn Jurayj.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿Say: "Who protects you?"﴾, that he said: "guards you." And concerning (p-937) His saying ﴿nor are they accompanied by Us﴾, he said: "They will not be helped." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿nor are they accompanied by Us﴾, that he said: "They will not be protected." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "They will not be prevented."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 44–56**

When he had refuted the claim that the idols benefit anyone, He turned to explaining that the good things they enjoy and the pleasures of the present life come from God, not from any protector who could keep them from destruction or any helper who could support them in obtaining these pleasures. So He said: ﴿Nay, We gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾, meaning the people of Makkah. God granted them enjoyment through the blessings He bestowed upon them ﴿until life was prolonged for them﴾. They were deceived by this and thought that they would continue in that state forever. God, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿Do they not see﴾, that is, do they not look and thus see ﴿that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾, by conquering it town after town and land after land. It has also been said that the reduction is by killing and taking captives. This matter has already been discussed fully in Surat al-Ra'd. The interrogative in His words ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ is for denial, and the fa' (then) is for coordination with an implied clause, like its counterparts. The meaning is: how could they be victorious after We have reduced their land from its outlying parts? In this there is an indication that the victors are the Muslims.

﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾, that is, I frighten you and caution you by the Qur'an. That is my task and what God has commanded me. As for His words ﴿nor do the deaf hear the call﴾, it may be part of the speech that the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to say to them, or it may be from God, exalted is He. The meaning is that whoever God has made deaf in his hearing, sealed his heart, and placed a covering over his sight, will not hear the call. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿wa-la yusma'u﴾ (and is not heard) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the mim, in the passive voice with the agent unnamed. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa and Yahya ibn al-Harith read it with a ta' (second person) with a damma and a kasra on the mim, meaning: you, O Muhammad, do not make these people hear. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: If it were as Ibn 'Amir said, the wording would be ﴿idha ma tundhiruhum﴾, which would be good in construction. But ﴿idha ma yundharun﴾ (when they are warned) is good in following the reading of the majority. The remaining readers read with a fatha on the ya' and a fatha on the mim, and a raf' (nominative) on "the deaf", making it the subject.

﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾. The word nafha (breath) here means a small amount, taken from the fragrance of musk, as Ibn Kaysan said. From this is the poet's saying:

*And a woman of the finest of women, her sleeves breathing out musk.*

Al-Mubarrad said: the nafha is a single push from a thing that is less than its main part. It is said: "he struck him with a nafha with the sword" if he struck him with a light blow. It has also been said that it is a jab, and it has been said that it is a glance. The meanings are close: that is, if even the least part of the punishment touches them, ﴿they will surely say: "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers"﴾, that is, they will call down woe and destruction upon themselves and confess their wrongdoing against themselves.

﴿And We shall set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection﴾. The word mawazin (scales) is the plural of mizan (scale), which indicates that there are several scales, though it is possible that one scale is meant and it is expressed in the plural form. What is sufficient about the description of the scale has been reported in the Sunnah, and it has been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, and what is in Surat al-Kahf on this matter suffices without repetition. The word qist (just) is an attribute of the scales. Al-Zajjaj said: qist is a verbal noun used as an attribute, as you say "a scale of qist" and "scales of qist". The meaning is "possessing justice", and qist means justice. It has been read as al-qisat with the sad and the ta'. The meaning of ﴿for the Day of Resurrection﴾ is "for the people of the Day of Resurrection". It has also been said that the lam means "in", that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾, that is, nothing will be reduced from the good of a doer of good, nor will anything be added to the evil of an evildoer. ﴿And even if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾. Nafi', Shayba and Abu Ja'far read mithqalu (weight) with a damma, making kana (was/be) complete, meaning: if it occurs or exists, the weight of a grain. The remaining readers read mithqala with a fatha, on the presumption: "and if the deed indicated by the placing of the scales is the weight of a grain". This was said by al-Zajjaj. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "and if the wrong is the weight of a grain". Al-Wahidi said: this is better because of the preceding words ﴿so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾. The weight of a thing is its scale, that is: even if it is in the utmost lightness and insignificance, since a grain of mustard seed is a proverb for smallness, ﴿We bring it﴾, that is, We bring it forth and come with it to requite for it. It is said: ata yu'ati mu'ata (to come, to requite), meaning "he requited". The majority read ﴿atayna﴾ with a short vowel (qasr), meaning: We bring it forth and come with it to requite for it. ﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾, that is: sufficient are We as counters. The original meaning of hasb is counting. It has also been said: sufficient are We as knowers, because whoever counts something knows it and preserves it. It has also been said: sufficient are We as requiters for what they put forward of good and evil.

Then He, glorified is He, began to explain in detail what He had summarized earlier in His words: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 7]. So He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾. The Criterion here means the Torah, because in it there is the distinction between the lawful and the unlawful. It has also been said that al-Furqan here is victory over the enemies, as in His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon Our servant on the Day of al-Furqan﴾ [al-Anfal: 41].

Al-Tha'labi said: this view is more similar to the apparent meaning of the verse. The meaning of ﴿and a light﴾ is that they were guided by it through the darkness of ignorance and error. The meaning of ﴿and a reminder﴾ is admonition, that is, they take heed by what is in it. He specified the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from it.

He described them with His words: (p-938) ﴿who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾, because this fear is inseparable from taqwa (piety). It is permissible that the relative clause be a substitute for "the God-fearing" or an explanation of it. The position of bil-ghayb (in the unseen) is accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, they fear His punishment while it is unseen by them, or they are absent from it because they are in this world and the punishment is in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima read ﴿diya'an﴾ (light) without the waw. Al-Farra' said: the waw was dropped, and bringing it is one and the same. Al-Zajjaj objected that the waw comes for a meaning and so is not added. ﴿And they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾, that is, they fear and are anxious about the Resurrection.

The reference in His words ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ is to the Qur'an. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that this Qur'an is a reminder for whoever takes heed by it and an admonition for whoever is admonished by it. "Blessed" means abundant in blessing and good. His words ﴿which We have sent down﴾ are a second attribute of "reminder", or a predicate after a predicate. The interrogative in His words ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾ is for denial, because of their denial: that is, how can you deny that it was sent down from God while you acknowledge that the Torah was sent down from Him?

﴿And We certainly gave Abraham his right guidance﴾, that is, the right guidance suitable for him and for the like of the messengers. The meaning of "from before" is that he was given his guidance before the giving of the Torah to Moses and Aaron. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that We gave him his guidance before prophethood, that is, We enabled him to reflect and reason when the night covered him and he saw the sun, the moon and the star. Most of the commentators hold this view, and a few hold the first view. ﴿And We were of him knowing﴾, that he was a fitting place for the giving of guidance and that he was suited for it. The adverbial phrase in His words ﴿When he said to his father﴾ is connected either to "We gave" or to an implied verb: that is, remember when he said. His father was Azar, and his people were Nimrod and those who followed him. The tamathil (images) are the idols. The root of timthal is a made thing resembling one of the created things of God, glorified is He. It is said: "I made the thing like the thing" when I made it resemble it, and the name of the thing made like another is timthal. He denounced their worship of them by saying: ﴿What are these images to which you are devoted?﴾ The word 'ukuf (devotion) is an expression for adhering to and persisting in a thing. The lam in la-ha (to them) is for specification. If it were for transitivity, the particle 'ala would have been used: that is, what are these idols upon whose worship you remain? It is also said that 'ukuf is implicit in the meaning of worship.

﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ They answered him with this answer, which is the staff that every weak person leans upon and the rope that every drowning person clings to, namely adherence to mere imitation of the fathers, that is: we found our fathers worshipping them, so we worshipped them, following them and walking in their way. Thus do these imitators among the people of this Islamic community answer, and when a scholar of the Book and the Sunnah denounces them for acting on pure opinion unsupported by evidence, they say: "This is what our imperam has said, whom we found our fathers imitating and taking his opinion." Their answer is what Abraham the Friend answered here.

﴿He said: "Indeed you were, you and your fathers, in manifest error."﴾ That is, in clear loss, evident and not hidden from anyone, and not confused to anyone of sound mind. Indeed the people of Abraham worshipped idols which neither harm nor benefit, neither hear nor see. There is no error after this error, and no loss equals this loss. As for these imitators among the people of Islam, they have substituted for the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger a book in which the independent judgments (ijtihad) of a scholar among the scholars of Islam have been recorded, who claimed that he did not come upon any evidence contradicting them, either because of his own deficiency or his negligence in research. Then whoever found that evidence and made it manifest, like a sign of light (or) a fire at the top of a mountain, was told: "This is the Book of God," or "this is the Sunnah of His Messenger." And they recited to them:

*Leave every saying in favour of the saying of Muhammad, for no one who is secure in his religion is like one who takes risks.*

So they said, as the first poet said:

*I am only of Ghazziyya: if Ghazziyya goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghazziyya is guided, I am guided.*

And one who said well:

*The youth refuses anything but following his desire, though the path of truth is clear to him.*

Then, when those people heard the statement of the Friend, ﴿they said: "Have you brought us the truth, or are you one of the jesters?"﴾, that is: are you serious in what you say, or are you a playful joker? He, turning away from what they based their statement upon of imitation, said: ﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them﴾, that is, created them and brought them into being ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that﴾ which I have mentioned to you, that your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth to the exclusion of whatever else, that is, I am of those who know it and provide proof of it. For the witness to a thing is one who knows it, proves it, and makes it clear.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir in his Tahdhib, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have reported from 'A'isha that a man said: "O Messenger of God, I have slaves who lie to me, betray me, and disobey me, and I beat them and abuse them. How am I regarding them?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Their betrayal, their disobedience and their lying to you will be reckoned, and your rebuke of them. If your punishment of them is less than their sins, it will be a favour to you; if your punishment of them is equal to their sins, it will be neither for you nor against you; and if your punishment of them exceeds their sins, retaliation will be taken from you for them." The man began to weep and cry out. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Have you not read the Book of God: ﴿And We shall set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection. So no soul will be wronged in anything. And even if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed, We bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾?" The man said: "O Messenger of God, I find nothing better for me and for them than separating from them. I call you to witness that they are free." This was narrated by Ahmad in this form: Abu Nuh al-Aqrad related to us: Layth ibn Sa'd informed us, from Malik ibn Anas, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, and he mentioned it. There are similar hadiths with this meaning.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to read: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light﴾. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abu Salih regarding ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion﴾ that he said: it is the Torah. Ibn Jarir reported similarly from Qatada. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd that he said: al-Furqan is the Truth. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada regarding ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ that it is the Qur'an. Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿And We certainly gave Abraham his right guidance﴾ that he said: We guided him as a child. And regarding His words ﴿What are these images﴾, he said: the idols.

Thus do these imitators among the people of this Islamic community answer, and when a scholar of the Book and the Sunnah denounces them for acting on pure opinion unsupported by evidence, they say: "This is what our imperam has said, whom we found our fathers imitating and taking his opinion." And regarding His words ﴿What are these images﴾, he said: the idols.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 21, verses 44–56**

When he had refuted the claim that the idols benefit anyone, He turned to explaining that the good things they enjoy and the pleasures of the present life come from God, not from any protector who could keep them from destruction or any helper who could support them in obtaining these pleasures. So He said: ﴿Nay, We gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾, meaning the people of Makkah. God granted them enjoyment through the blessings He bestowed upon them ﴿until life was prolonged for them﴾. They were deceived by this and thought that they would continue in that state forever. God, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿Do they not see﴾, that is, do they not look and thus see ﴿that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾, by conquering it town after town and land after land. It has also been said that the reduction is by killing and taking captives. This matter has already been discussed fully in Surat al-Ra'd. The interrogative in His words ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ is for denial, and the fa' (then) is for coordination with an implied clause, like its counterparts. The meaning is: how could they be victorious after We have reduced their land from its outlying parts? In this there is an indication that the victors are the Muslims.

﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾, that is, I frighten you and caution you by the Qur'an. That is my task and what God has commanded me. As for His words ﴿nor do the deaf hear the call﴾, it may be part of the speech that the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to say to them, or it may be from God, exalted is He. The meaning is that whoever God has made deaf in his hearing, sealed his heart, and placed a covering over his sight, will not hear the call. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿wa-la yusma'u﴾ (and is not heard) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the mim, in the passive voice with the agent unnamed. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa and Yahya ibn al-Harith read it with a ta' (second person) with a damma and a kasra on the mim, meaning: you, O Muhammad, do not make these people hear. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: If it were as Ibn 'Amir said, the wording would be ﴿idha ma tundhiruhum﴾, which would be good in construction. But ﴿idha ma yundharun﴾ (when they are warned) is good in following the reading of the majority. The remaining readers read with a fatha on the ya' and a fatha on the mim, and a raf' (nominative) on "the deaf", making it the subject.

﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾. The word nafha (breath) here means a small amount, taken from the fragrance of musk, as Ibn Kaysan said. From this is the poet's saying:

*And a woman of the finest of women, her sleeves breathing out musk.*

Al-Mubarrad said: the nafha is a single push from a thing that is less than its main part. It is said: "he struck him with a nafha with the sword" if he struck him with a light blow. It has also been said that it is a jab, and it has been said that it is a glance. The meanings are close: that is, if even the least part of the punishment touches them, ﴿they will surely say: "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers"﴾, that is, they will call down woe and destruction upon themselves and confess their wrongdoing against themselves.

﴿And We shall set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection﴾. The word mawazin (scales) is the plural of mizan (scale), which indicates that there are several scales, though it is possible that one scale is meant and it is expressed in the plural form. What is sufficient about the description of the scale has been reported in the Sunnah, and it has been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, and what is in Surat al-Kahf on this matter suffices without repetition. The word qist (just) is an attribute of the scales. Al-Zajjaj said: qist is a verbal noun used as an attribute, as you say "a scale of qist" and "scales of qist". The meaning is "possessing justice", and qist means justice. It has been read as al-qisat with the sad and the ta'. The meaning of ﴿for the Day of Resurrection﴾ is "for the people of the Day of Resurrection". It has also been said that the lam means "in", that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾, that is, nothing will be reduced from the good of a doer of good, nor will anything be added to the evil of an evildoer. ﴿And even if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾. Nafi', Shayba and Abu Ja'far read mithqalu (weight) with a damma, making kana (was/be) complete, meaning: if it occurs or exists, the weight of a grain. The remaining readers read mithqala with a fatha, on the presumption: "and if the deed indicated by the placing of the scales is the weight of a grain". This was said by al-Zajjaj. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "and if the wrong is the weight of a grain". Al-Wahidi said: this is better because of the preceding words ﴿so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾. The weight of a thing is its scale, that is: even if it is in the utmost lightness and insignificance, since a grain of mustard seed is a proverb for smallness, ﴿We bring it﴾, that is, We bring it forth and come with it to requite for it. It is said: ata yu'ati mu'ata (to come, to requite), meaning "he requited". The majority read ﴿atayna﴾ with a short vowel (qasr), meaning: We bring it forth and come with it to requite for it. ﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾, that is: sufficient are We as counters. The original meaning of hasb is counting. It has also been said: sufficient are We as knowers, because whoever counts something knows it and preserves it. It has also been said: sufficient are We as requiters for what they put forward of good and evil.

Then He, glorified is He, began to explain in detail what He had summarized earlier in His words: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 7]. So He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾. The Criterion here means the Torah, because in it there is the distinction between the lawful and the unlawful. It has also been said that al-Furqan here is victory over the enemies, as in His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon Our servant on the Day of al-Furqan﴾ [al-Anfal: 41].

Al-Tha'labi said: this view is more similar to the apparent meaning of the verse. The meaning of ﴿and a light﴾ is that they were guided by it through the darkness of ignorance and error. The meaning of ﴿and a reminder﴾ is admonition, that is, they take heed by what is in it. He specified the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from it.

He described them with His words: (p-938) ﴿who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾, because this fear is inseparable from taqwa (piety). It is permissible that the relative clause be a substitute for "the God-fearing" or an explanation of it. The position of bil-ghayb (in the unseen) is accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, they fear His punishment while it is unseen by them, or they are absent from it because they are in this world and the punishment is in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima read ﴿diya'an﴾ (light) without the waw. Al-Farra' said: the waw was dropped, and bringing it is one and the same. Al-Zajjaj objected that the waw comes for a meaning and so is not added. ﴿And they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾, that is, they fear and are anxious about the Resurrection.

The reference in His words ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ is to the Qur'an. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that this Qur'an is a reminder for whoever takes heed by it and an admonition for whoever is admonished by it. "Blessed" means abundant in blessing and good. His words ﴿which We have sent down﴾ are a second attribute of "reminder", or a predicate after a predicate. The interrogative in His words ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾ is for denial, because of their denial: that is, how can you deny that it was sent down from God while you acknowledge that the Torah was sent down from Him?

(p-٩٣٩).

His saying, ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾: he informed them that he would move from argument by speech to changing the wrong by action, trusting in God, may He be glorified, and defending His religion. Al-kayd (scheming) means plotting. One says *kadahu yakiduhu kaydan wa makidatan*. What is meant here is striving to break the idols. It was said that he said this in secret, and it was said that a man among them heard him. ﴿After you have turned your backs and gone away﴾ means after you have returned from worshipping them, departing and going off.

The exegetes said: They had a festival every year that they would gather for, and they said to Abraham, "If you came out with us to our festival, our religion would please you." Abraham then made this statement. The fa' in His saying ﴿and he reduced them to fragments﴾ is *fasiha* (an explanatory connective), meaning: so they turned away, and he reduced them to fragments. Al-judhadh means cutting and breaking. One says *jadhadhtu al-shay'* (I cut the thing) and *kasartuhu* (I broke it). The singular is *judhadhah*, and *al-judhadh* is what has been broken from it. Al-Jawhari said: al-Kisa'i said, "Gold stones are called *al-judhadh* because they are broken."

Al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read (جِذاذًا) *jidhadhan* with a kasra on the jim, meaning breaking and cutting. It is the plural of *jadhidh*, which is crumbled debris, like *khafif* and *khifaf*, and *zarif* and *zirif*.

The poet said:
"He smashed the idols in their sanctuary; that was for the sake of God, the Exalted, the Mighty."

The rest read it with a damma. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, meaning the debris and the fragments, the form *fi'al* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). This is the scheme he had promised them.

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Simak read (جَذاذًا) *jadhadhan* with a fatha on the jim. ﴿Except their chief﴾ means except the chief of the idols. ﴿So that they might turn to it﴾ means so that they might turn to Abraham, and he would argue against them with what will come, and so he would overcome them. It was also said: so that they might turn to the large idol and ask it about the one who broke them, because it is the nature of a worshipped deity that matters be referred to it. When they return to it they will find no news with it, and then they will know that it cannot bring benefit or ward off harm, and that it knows neither good nor evil and does not inform about what befalls it. It was also said: so that they might turn to God, but this is very far-fetched.

﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? He is surely one of the wrongdoers."﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech. The implied meaning is: when they returned from their festival and saw what had happened to their gods, they said this statement. The interrogative is for rebuke. It was also said that *man* is not interrogative, but is the subject, and its predicate is *innahu la-mina al-zalimin* (he is surely one of the wrongdoers), meaning: the doer of this is a wrongdoer.

The first view is preferable because of their saying, ﴿We heard a youth mention them, called Abraham﴾, etc., for one of them said this in answer to those who questioned them. This speaker is the one who heard Abraham say, ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols.﴾ The meaning of *yadhkuruhum* (mention them) is to disparage them. The phrase has been explained before. The clause ﴿called Abraham﴾ is a second attribute of *fatan* (a youth). Al-Zajjaj said: *Ibrahim* is in the nominative on the basis of the meaning: "He is called, 'He is Abraham'." So on this view it is the predicate of an omitted subject. It was also said that its nominative status is because it is the subject of a passive verb (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu*, the passive construction whose agent is not named), and it was said that it is nominative as a vocative. Among the strange grammatical refinements and wondrous i'rab (grammatical parsing) interpretations is that al-A'lam al-Shantamari al-Ishbili said that it is nominative by *al-ihmal* (an unattached, independent nominative). Ibn 'Atiyya said: he went to its nominative status without any reason. *Al-fata* is the young man, and *al-fatah* is the young woman.

﴿They said, "Bring him before the eyes of the people."﴾ The speakers are the questioners. They ordered some of them to bring him openly, in sight of the people. It was said that when the news reached Nimrod and the nobles of his people, they disliked seizing him without evidence, so they said this statement so that it would be a proof against him, by which they would make lawful what they had resolved to do to him. The meaning of ﴿so that they may bear witness﴾ is so that they may attend his punishment, so that others would be deterred from following his example in such a matter. It was also said: so that they may bear witness against him that they saw him breaking the idols, or so that they may witness his reviling of their idols.

The clause ﴿They said, "Did you do this to our gods, O Abraham?"﴾ is a resumptive statement answering an implied question. The speech contains an ellipsis, its implied sense being: Abraham came when they brought him, and they questioned him whether he had done that, in order to establish the proof against him according to their claim. ﴿He said, "Rather, this one, their chief, did it."﴾ That is, Abraham said, establishing the proof against them and rebuking them: "Rather, this, their chief, did it," pointing to the idol that he had left and had not broken. ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾ means: if they are among those who are able to speak, who are capable of speech and understand what is said to them, so that they answer with what corresponds to it. It is not sound by reason to attribute divinity to it.

So the speech was given the form of an indirect challenge to them, by which they would be led to acknowledge that the inanimate things they worshipped are not gods. For when they said that they cannot speak, he said to them: then how do you worship one who is incapable of speech and falls short of knowing what occurs before it in the place where it is? This speech is of the kind of supposing falsehood with the opponent until the proof binds him and he acknowledges the truth, for that is most cutting to his doubt and most effective in repelling his obstinacy. It was also said: by attributing the act to that great one among the idols, Abraham, peace be upon him, intended that it did this because it was jealous and angry that it was worshipped while the small ones were worshipped along with it, as guidance for them to the fact that worshipping these idols, which do not hear, see, benefit or ward off harm, is not reasonable, given the existence of their Creator and theirs. But the first view is preferable. Ibn al-Sumayfi' read (بَلْ فَعَلَّهُ) *bal fa'allahu* with a shadda on the lam, meaning: "Rather, perhaps the doer is their chief."

﴿Then they returned to themselves﴾ means some of them returned to others, the return of one who is cut off from his argument, who realizes the validity of his opponent's argument and returns to his reason. That is because they became aware and understood during this exchange between them and Abraham that one who cannot repel harm from (p-٩٤٠) himself, nor inflict harm on the one who did to him what Abraham did to those idols, is impossible to be deserving of worship. Therefore ﴿they said, "You yourselves are the wrongdoers."﴾ That is, some of them said to others: You are the wrongdoers against yourselves by worshipping these inanimate things. The wrongdoer is not the one you attributed wrongdoing to by your saying, "He is surely one of the wrongdoers."

﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads﴾ means they returned to their ignorance and obstinacy. He, may He be glorified, compared their return to falsehood to the lower part of a thing becoming its upper part. It was also said that the meaning is: they lowered their heads out of embarrassment before Abraham. But this is weak, because He did not say *nakasu ru'usahum* (they lowered their heads) with a fatha on the kaf and the verb attributed to them, so that this interpretation would be valid. Rather He said *nukisu 'ala ru'usihim* (they were overturned upon their heads). It was read *nukkisu* with a shadda. Then, after they were overturned, they said addressing Abraham: ﴿You surely know that these do not speak.﴾ That is, saying to Abraham: "You surely know that speech is not among the qualities of these idols." ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, besides God, that which cannot benefit you in any way, nor harm you with any kind of harm?"﴾ Abraham, rebuking them and disparaging them, then became impatient with them, peace be upon him, and said: ﴿Uff to you, and to what you worship besides God!﴾ In this is belittling of them and their objects of worship. The *lam* in *lakum* indicates the one for whom the exclamation is made: that is, for you and for your gods. *Al-ta'affuf* is a sound indicating impatience. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is, you have no minds with which you reflect, so that you would know this vile act that you have committed.

When the people returned from their festival, they entered and found their gods broken, and the largest of them with the instrument that had smashed the idols in its hand. But this is weak, because He did not say *nakasu ru'usahum* (they lowered their heads) with a fatha on the kaf and the verb attributed to them, so that this interpretation would be valid. Rather He said *nukisu 'ala ru'usihim* (they were overturned upon their heads). It was read *nukkisu* with a shadda. Then, after they were overturned, they said addressing Abraham: ﴿You surely know that these do not speak.﴾ That is, saying to Abraham: "You surely know that speech is not among the qualities of these idols." ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, besides God, that which cannot benefit you in any way, nor harm you with any kind of harm?"﴾ Abraham, rebuking them and disparaging them, then became impatient with them, peace be upon him, and said: ﴿Uff to you, and to what you worship besides God!﴾ In this is belittling of them and their objects of worship. The *lam* in *lakum* indicates the one for whom the exclamation is made: that is, for you and for your gods. *Al-ta'affuf* is a sound indicating impatience. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is, you have no minds with which you reflect, so that you would know this vile act that you have committed.

﴿They said, "Burn him!"﴾ That is, some of them said to others when they were at a loss to repel Abraham, and unable to dispute with him, and the ways of debate were closed to them: burn Abraham, turning toward the path of oppression and brute force, and inclining toward showing dominance by whatever means and in whatever matter came to hand. For this reason they said, ﴿and support your gods, if you are going to act﴾, meaning: support them by taking revenge on the one who did to them what he did, if you are indeed going to act to give support. It was said that this speaker was Nimrod, and it was said: a man from the Kurds.

﴿We said, "O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham!"﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied meaning being: they kindled the fire and took Abraham to it. At that point We said, "O fire, be cool and safe." It was said that *salaman* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) of an omitted verb, meaning: "And We made it safe for him, a safety." ﴿They intended a scheme against him﴾, that is, a plot. ﴿So We made them the greatest losers﴾, that is, losers greater than every loser. We turned their plot back upon them, and We gave them the outcome of evil, just as We gave Abraham the outcome of good.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: When Abraham's people went out to their festival, they passed by him and said, "O Abraham, will you not come out with us?" He said, "I am sick," and he had been well the day before. He said, ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned your backs and gone away.﴾ Some of them heard him. When they had gone out, he went to his household, took some food, and then went to their gods and placed it before them, saying, "Will you not eat?" Then he smashed them, all except the largest of them, and he tied the instrument he had used to smash them to its hand. When the people returned from their festival, they entered and found their gods broken, and the largest of them with the instrument that had smashed the idols in its hand. They said, "Who has done this to our gods?" Those who had heard Abraham saying, ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols,﴾ said, ﴿We heard a young man mentioning them,﴾ and at that point Abraham debated with them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿judhadhan﴾ (in pieces), that he said: "Hutaman," meaning fragments. Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "Futatan," meaning crumbs. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him, regarding ﴿Rather, their largest one did it, this one﴾, that he said: "The greatest of their gods."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayra that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abraham never lied in anything except three instances, all of them concerning Allah: his saying, 'I am sick,' when he was not sick; his saying to Sarah, 'She is my sister'; and his saying, ﴿Rather, their largest one did it, this one.﴾" This hadith is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, in a longer form than this. Abu Ya'la related something similar from the hadith of Abu Sa'd.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: When everything that was gathered for Abraham had been gathered and he was thrown into the fire, the keeper of the rain began saying, "When am I commanded to send the rain so that I may send it?" But the command of Allah was faster. Allah said, ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety,﴾ and no fire remained on earth except that it was extinguished.

Ahmad, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani related from A'isha that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Abraham was thrown into the fire, there was no living creature except that it was extinguishing the fire from him, except the gecko (wazagh), for it was blowing upon Abraham. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that it be killed."

Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Musannaf and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Umar that he said: The first words Abraham said when he was thrown into the fire were: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿O fire, be coolness,﴾ that he said: "It was Gabriel who called to it."

Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Had He not followed its coolness with safety, Abraham would have died from its coldness."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ali something similar to this.

Ibn Jarir related from Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman al-Taymi, from some of his companions, that he said: Gabriel came to Abraham while he was being bound to be thrown into the fire, and said, "O Abraham, do you have any need?" He said, "As for you, no."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ka'b that he said: The fire burned nothing of Abraham except his bonds.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Minhal ibn Amr that he said: I was told that Abraham was thrown into the fire and remained in it for either fifty or forty (days). He said: "I never spent days and nights more pleasant in life than the time I spent in it. I wished that my whole life and existence were like my life while I was in it."

(p-٩٣٩).

His saying, ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾: he informed them that he would move from argument by speech to changing the wrong by action, trusting in God, may He be glorified, and defending His religion. Al-kayd (scheming) means plotting. One says *kadahu yakiduhu kaydan wa makidatan*. What is meant here is striving to break the idols. It was said that he said this in secret, and it was said that a man among them heard him. ﴿After you have turned your backs and gone away﴾ means after you have returned from worshipping them, departing and going off.

The exegetes said: They had a festival every year that they would gather for, and they said to Abraham, "If you came out with us to our festival, our religion would please you." Abraham then made this statement. The fa' in His saying ﴿and he reduced them to fragments﴾ is *fasiha* (an explanatory connective), meaning: so they turned away, and he reduced them to fragments. Al-judhadh means cutting and breaking. One says *jadhadhtu al-shay'* (I cut the thing) and *kasartuhu* (I broke it). The singular is *judhadhah*, and *al-judhadh* is what has been broken from it. Al-Jawhari said: al-Kisa'i said, "Gold stones are called *al-judhadh* because they are broken."

Al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read (جِذاذًا) *jidhadhan* with a kasra on the jim, meaning breaking and cutting. It is the plural of *jadhidh*, which is crumbled debris, like *khafif* and *khifaf*, and *zarif* and *zirif*.

The poet said:
"He smashed the idols in their sanctuary; that was for the sake of God, the Exalted, the Mighty."

The rest read it with a damma. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, meaning the debris and the fragments, the form *fi'al* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). This is the scheme he had promised them.

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Simak read (جَذاذًا) *jadhadhan* with a fatha on the jim. ﴿Except their chief﴾ means except the chief of the idols. ﴿So that they might turn to it﴾ means so that they might turn to Abraham, and he would argue against them with what will come, and so he would overcome them. It was also said: so that they might turn to the large idol and ask it about the one who broke them, because it is the nature of a worshipped deity that matters be referred to it. When they return to it they will find no news with it, and then they will know that it cannot bring benefit or ward off harm, and that it knows neither good nor evil and does not inform about what befalls it. It was also said: so that they might turn to God, but this is very far-fetched.

﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? He is surely one of the wrongdoers."﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech. The implied meaning is: when they returned from their festival and saw what had happened to their gods, they said this statement. The interrogative is for rebuke. It was also said that *man* is not interrogative, but is the subject, and its predicate is *innahu la-mina al-zalimin* (he is surely one of the wrongdoers), meaning: the doer of this is a wrongdoer.

The first view is preferable because of their saying, ﴿We heard a youth mention them, called Abraham﴾, etc., for one of them said this in answer to those who questioned them. This speaker is the one who heard Abraham say, ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols.﴾ The meaning of *yadhkuruhum* (mention them) is to disparage them. The phrase has been explained before. The clause ﴿called Abraham﴾ is a second attribute of *fatan* (a youth). Al-Zajjaj said: *Ibrahim* is in the nominative on the basis of the meaning: "He is called, 'He is Abraham'." So on this view it is the predicate of an omitted subject. It was also said that its nominative status is because it is the subject of a passive verb (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu*, the passive construction whose agent is not named), and it was said that it is nominative as a vocative. Among the strange grammatical refinements and wondrous i'rab (grammatical parsing) interpretations is that al-A'lam al-Shantamari al-Ishbili said that it is nominative by *al-ihmal* (an unattached, independent nominative). Ibn 'Atiyya said: he went to its nominative status without any reason. *Al-fata* is the young man, and *al-fatah* is the young woman.

﴿They said, "Bring him before the eyes of the people."﴾ The speakers are the questioners. They ordered some of them to bring him openly, in sight of the people. It was said that when the news reached Nimrod and the nobles of his people, they disliked seizing him without evidence, so they said this statement so that it would be a proof against him, by which they would make lawful what they had resolved to do to him. The meaning of ﴿so that they may bear witness﴾ is so that they may attend his punishment, so that others would be deterred from following his example in such a matter. It was also said: so that they may bear witness against him that they saw him breaking the idols, or so that they may witness his reviling of their idols.

The clause ﴿They said, "Did you do this to our gods, O Abraham?"﴾ is a resumptive statement answering an implied question. The speech contains an ellipsis, its implied sense being: Abraham came when they brought him, and they questioned him whether he had done that, in order to establish the proof against him according to their claim. ﴿He said, "Rather, this one, their chief, did it."﴾ That is, Abraham said, establishing the proof against them and rebuking them: "Rather, this, their chief, did it," pointing to the idol that he had left and had not broken. ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾ means: if they are among those who are able to speak, who are capable of speech and understand what is said to them, so that they answer with what corresponds to it. It is not sound by reason to attribute divinity to it.

So the speech was given the form of an indirect challenge to them, by which they would be led to acknowledge that the inanimate things they worshipped are not gods. For when they said that they cannot speak, he said to them: then how do you worship one who is incapable of speech and falls short of knowing what occurs before it in the place where it is? This speech is of the kind of supposing falsehood with the opponent until the proof binds him and he acknowledges the truth, for that is most cutting to his doubt and most effective in repelling his obstinacy. It was also said: by attributing the act to that great one among the idols, Abraham, peace be upon him, intended that it did this because it was jealous and angry that it was worshipped while the small ones were worshipped along with it, as guidance for them to the fact that worshipping these idols, which do not hear, see, benefit or ward off harm, is not reasonable, given the existence of their Creator and theirs. But the first view is preferable. Ibn al-Sumayfi' read (بَلْ فَعَلَّهُ) *bal fa'allahu* with a shadda on the lam, meaning: "Rather, perhaps the doer is their chief."

﴿Then they returned to themselves﴾ means some of them returned to others, the return of one who is cut off from his argument, who realizes the validity of his opponent's argument and returns to his reason. That is because they became aware and understood during this exchange between them and Abraham that one who cannot repel harm from (p-٩٤٠) himself, nor inflict harm on the one who did to him what Abraham did to those idols, is impossible to be deserving of worship. Therefore ﴿they said, "You yourselves are the wrongdoers."﴾ That is, some of them said to others: You are the wrongdoers against yourselves by worshipping these inanimate things. The wrongdoer is not the one you attributed wrongdoing to by your saying, "He is surely one of the wrongdoers."

﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads﴾ means they returned to their ignorance and obstinacy. He, may He be glorified, compared their return to falsehood to the lower part of a thing becoming its upper part. It was also said that the meaning is: they lowered their heads out of embarrassment before Abraham. But this is weak, because He did not say *nakasu ru'usahum* (they lowered their heads) with a fatha on the kaf and the verb attributed to them, so that this interpretation would be valid. Rather He said *nukisu 'ala ru'usihim* (they were overturned upon their heads). It was read *nukkisu* with a shadda. But the command of Allah was faster. Allah said, ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety,﴾ and no fire remained on earth except that it was extinguished.
