Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger﴾, that he said: "He became angry with his people." ﴿And he thought that We would not have power over him﴾, meaning: that We would not decree a punishment or a trial upon him for what he did to his people in his anger toward them and his fleeing. He said: "His punishment was that the whale seized him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And he thought that We would not have power over him﴾, that he said: "He thought that the punishment that befell him would not seize him."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿And he called out in the darknesses﴾, that he said: "The darkness of the night, the darkness of the belly of the whale, and the darkness of the sea."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The supplication of Dhu al-Nun when he was in the belly of the whale: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." No Muslim has ever called upon his Lord with it concerning anything except that He has responded to him.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The Name of Allah by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives, is the supplication of Yunus ibn Matta.'" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this specific to Yunus, or to the whole community of Muslims?" He said: "It is specific to Yunus, and general for the believers when they call upon Him with it. Have you not heard the words of Allah: ﴿And thus We deliver the believers﴾? So it is a condition from Allah for whoever calls upon Him with it."

al-Hakim narrated a similar report from his (Ibn Abbas's) narration as well. It is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not proper for anyone to say: 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta.'" It is also narrated in the Sahih and elsewhere from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is also narrated in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 21, verses 78–88 (part 1 of 3):

.
His saying: "Dawud" is conjoined to "Nuh" and is an object governed by its governing verb, either the one mentioned or the one implied, as has passed. "Sulayman" is conjoined to "Dawud." The adverbial phrase in ﴿when they both judged﴾ is connected to what governed "Dawud," meaning: mention them at the time of their judgment. The purpose of mentioning them is to mention their story. The meaning of ﴿concerning the tilth﴾ is "regarding the matter of the tilth." It was said: it was a field of crops; it was said: a vineyard; and the term "harth" (tilth) applies to both. ﴿When the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾ means they scattered and spread out in it. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-nafsh" (with a vowel on the first letter) is when sheep spread out at night without a shepherd. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ means to the judgment of the two judges. In this there is the permissibility of using the plural for two, which is the view of a group of Arabic grammarians such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Radi, and al-Farra' preceded both of them in saying this. It was said: (p-٩٤٢) the intended meaning is the two judges and the one judged against, and "witnesses" means present. The clause is parenthetical.

The clause ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾ is conjoined to "when they both judged," because that is in the sense of the past. The pronoun in "fafahhamnaha" (We gave understanding of it) refers to the matter understood from the speech, or to the judgment indicated by the mention of the ruling.

The exegetes said: two men entered upon Dawud, and with him was his son Sulayman. One of them was the owner of a field, and the other the owner of sheep. The owner of the field said: "This man's sheep got loose at night, entered my field, and left nothing of it." He said: "You are entitled to the sheep as compensation." Sulayman said: "Or something other than that: the owners of the vineyard should take the sheep, benefit from their milk and produce, and the owners of the sheep should tend the vineyard. Then, when it returns to its condition, as on the night the sheep strayed into it, they will return each one's property to its owner." Dawud said: "The judgment is what you have decided," and he ruled accordingly. Al-Nahhas said: Dawud only ruled the sheep for the owner of the field because their price was close to his loss. As for Sulayman's ruling, it was said: the value of what the sheep took and the value of what they destroyed were equal.

A group of scholars said: Dawud judged by revelation, and Sulayman judged by revelation, a revelation by which God abrogated Dawud's ruling. Thus the "understanding" in this view is by way of revelation. The majority said: their judgment was by ijtihad (independent reasoning, the exertion of a qualified jurist to derive a ruling). The discussion of the judgment of the prophets' ijtihad is well known, and likewise what the scholars mentioned concerning the disagreement of mujtahids (qualified jurists exercising ijtihad): is every mujtahid correct, or is the truth with one of them? Those who argue that every mujtahid is correct have cited this verse, but this verse does not indicate that, nor does any other. Rather, the hadith agreed upon in the two Sahihs and others explicitly states that when a judge strives and is correct, he has two rewards, and if he strives and errs, he has one reward. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, called him "mistaken" (mukhti', one who errs). So how can it be said that he is correct in matching the judgment of God? For the judgment of God, Glorified is He, is one and does not differ according to the differences of mujtahids. Otherwise it would follow that His judgment depends on the ijtihad of mujtahids, and the implication is false, so the implicating thing is likewise false. Also it would be implied that the thing concerning which the mujtahids differed as to its being lawful or unlawful is lawful in the judgment of God, Glorified is He. This implication: every mujtahid has an ijtihad in that case, and what God, Glorified is He, wills concerning it does not end except with the end of the mujtahids. The implication is false, so the implicating thing is likewise false. We have clarified this question with what has no addition to it in the work we named "al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid" (The Beneficial Word on the Ruling of Taqlid) and "Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab" (The Etiquette of Seeking and the Final Aim). Whoever wishes to verify the truth should refer to those two.

If you say: what is the ruling of this incident, in which Dawud and Sulayman judged, under this Muhammadan Shari'ah and the Islamic religion? I say: it has been established from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, through the hadith of al-Bara' that he legislated for his community that the owners of livestock must guard them at night, and the owners of orchards must guard them by day, and that what livestock destroy at night is a liability upon their owners. This liability is the amount of what was lost, either in kind or in value. The majority of scholars have acted upon what this hadith contains. Abu Hanifa, his companions, and a group of the Kufans held that this ruling was abrogated, and that when animals destroy crops by night or by day, their owner is not obligated to anything. They included the destruction of animals within the generality of the Prophet's saying, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: "The wound caused by an animal is unpaid" (jurh al-'ajma' jubar), analogizing all of their actions to their wounding (qiyas, analogical reasoning). It is answered that this analogy is invalid, because it stands against the explicit text. Some scholars held that the owner of the livestock is liable for what they destroy, without distinction between night and day. It is answered by the hadith of al-Bara'. And among what indicates that these two rulings of Dawud and Sulayman were by revelation from God, Glorified is He, and not by ijtihad, is the following.

His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. God, Glorified is He, informed us that He gave each of them these two matters. If they are specific, then their applicability to this case which God related about them takes precedence over their applicability to other cases. If they are general, then this instance of judgment and knowledge, which occurred from each of them in this case, is the most appropriate of the individual cases of that general term to be included under it and to be indicated by it. From this it is derived that what might be suggested by specifying Sulayman with understanding is dispelled, namely that Dawud's ruling was not a legal ruling. That is: each of them We gave judgment and abundant knowledge, not Sulayman alone.

When He praised Dawud and Sulayman together, He then mentioned what is specific to each of them. He began with Dawud, saying: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] with Dawud﴾. The glorification (tasbih) is either literal or figurative. A group held the first view, and it is the apparent meaning. That is because when Dawud glorified, the mountains glorified with him. It was said that they prayed with him when he prayed, and that is the meaning of glorification. Another group held the figurative view and interpreted the glorification as the glorification of one who sees them in wonder at the greatness of their creation and the power of their Creator. It was said that the mountains would move with Dawud, and whoever saw them moving with him glorified God. "And the birds" is conjoined to "the mountains." It is also read in the nominative, as a subject with an omitted predicate: "and the birds are subjected." Conjunction to the pronoun in "yusabbihna" is not valid, because there is no emphasis and no separation. ﴿And We were ever doers﴾ means what has been mentioned: the giving of understanding, the bestowing of judgment, and the subjugation.

﴿And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail for you﴾. Al-labus, in the Arabs' usage, is all weaponry, whether a coat of mail, a cuirass, a sword, or a spear. Al-Hudhali said: "And with me is a labus among garments, as if it were..." etc. The meaning in the verse is specifically coats of mail, and it is in the sense of "the thing worn," like "rakub" (ridden) and "halub" (milked). The prepositional phrase "for you" is connected to "We taught." ﴿That He might protect you from your violence﴾. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, and Rawh read "li-tuhassinakum" with the letter ta' on top, referring the pronoun to the craft, or to "labus" with the interpretation of "the coat of mail." Shayba, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "li-nuhassinakum" with nun, referring the pronoun to Him, Glorified is He. The rest read with ya', referring the pronoun to "labus," or to Dawud, or to God, Glorified is He. The meaning of "min ba'sikum" is "from your war," or "from the striking of weapons upon you." ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ for this blessing which We have bestowed upon you. The interrogative is in the sense of a command.

Then He mentioned what was specific to Sulayman. He said: ﴿And to Sulayman the wind﴾. That is, We subjected to him the wind, violent, that is, strong in its blowing. It is said: "the wind became violent," meaning it grew strong, so it is a violent wind (rih 'asif) and 'asuf. The accusative of "al-rih" is by way of circumstance. 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, al-Sulami, and Abu Bakr read "wa-li-Sulayman al-rihu" with the nominative on "al-rih," as a new beginning, and it is the subject with its predicate "tajri" (runs). As for the reading of the accusative, the position of "tajri bi-amrihi" (it runs by his command) is also accusative, as a circumstance or as a substitute, ﴿to the land which We had blessed﴾, which is the land of Syria, as has passed before. ﴿And We were ever knowing of all things﴾, that is, of the destruction of every thing.

﴿And of the devils﴾, that is, We subjected from among the devils those who dive for him in the seas and bring up from them what he sought from them. It was said that "min" is a subject whose predicate is what precedes it. Diving (al-ghawsh) is descending beneath the water; one says "ghasa fi al-ma'" (he dived into the water), and a ghawwas is one who dives in the sea for pearls. ﴿And they did works other than that﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, other than that. It was said: he meant by that the prayer niches (mahareeb), statues, and other things for which he subjected them. ﴿And We were ever guardians over them﴾, that is, over their works. Al-Farra' said: guarding them from fleeing or from refusing, or We guarded them from departing from His command. Al-Zajjaj said: He used to guard them from spoiling what they had done, and their habit was to spoil by night what they had done by day.

﴿And Ayyub, when he called upon his Lord﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and its governing verb is either what is mentioned or what is implied, as has passed. The governing verb of the adverbial phrase, namely "when he called upon his Lord," is the same governing verb of Ayyub. ﴿That harm has touched me﴾, that is, "that harm has touched me." It was read with the kasra on "inni." ﴿The harm which befell him is disputed: it was said that he got up to pray and could not rise. It was said that he acknowledged his incapacity, so that this would not contradict patience. It was said that revelation was cut off from him for forty days. It was said that a worm fell from his flesh, and he picked it up and returned it to its place, and it ate from him, so he cried out "harm has touched me." It was said that worms took hold of his body, and he endured until a worm reached his heart. It was said that his harm was the saying of Iblis to his wife: "Prostrate to me," and he feared the loss of her faith. It was said that his people loathed him. It was said that by harm he meant mockery. It was said other than that.

When he called upon his Lord humbly, he described Him with the utmost mercy, saying: ﴿And You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾. So God, Glorified is He, informed of His responding to his supplication, saying: ﴿So We responded to him, and removed what harm was upon him﴾, that is, God healed him of what he had, and compensated him for what he had lost. For this reason He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. It was said that God left them for him and gave him the like of them in this world. Al-Nahhas said: the attribution of this is correct, and his family had all died except his wife, so God restored them in less than the blink of an eye, and gave him the like of them along with them. It was said that this was by his having a number of children double those whom God had caused to die, so the meaning of the verse according to this is: We gave him the like of his family and the like of them with them. The accusative of ﴿a mercy from Us﴾ is by way of cause: that is, We gave him that out of Our mercy to him. ﴿And a reminder for the worshippers﴾, that is, and a reminder to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient. It is disputed how long he remained under the affliction: it was said seven years, seven months, seven days, and seven nights; it was said thirty years; it was said eighteen years.

﴿And Isma'il, and Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl﴾, that is, mention these. Idris is Enoch (Akhnukh), and Dhu al-Kifl is Ilyas (Elias). It was said he was Yusha' ibn Nun, it was said Zakariyya. The correct view is that he was a man from the Children of Israel who did not refrain from any of the sins, then he repented, and God forgave him. It was said that when al-Yasa' grew old he said: "Who will undertake for me such and such of the qualities of good, so that I may appoint him as my successor?" A man said: "I will." So he appointed him, and he was named Dhu al-Kifl. It was said he was a man who would take responsibility for the affairs of every person when he fell into any of the important matters. It was said other than that. The majority have held that he was not a prophet, and a group said he was a prophet. Then God, Glorified is He, described these by patience, saying: ﴿Each of them was of the patient﴾, that is, each one of these was among the patient in carrying out what God had obligated them to.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 21, verses 78–88 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾, that is, into Paradise, or into prophethood, or into goodness in its general sense. Then he gave the reason for that in His words: ﴿Indeed, they were among the righteous﴾, that is, those perfect in righteousness.

And [mention] Dhu al-Nun (Dhu al-Nun, "the man of the fish"), that is, mention Dhu al-Nun, who is Yunus ibn Matta. He was given the title Dhu al-Nun because the fish swallowed him, for *al-nun* is one of the names of the fish. It has also been said that he was called Dhu al-Nun because he saw a beautiful child and said: "Make his *nunah* dark, lest the evil eye afflict him." Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that the *nunah* of a child is the soft spot found on the chin of a small child. The meaning of *dassimu* ("make dark") is *sawwidu* ("blacken"). ﴿When he went off in anger﴾, that is, mention Dhu al-Nun at the time when he went off *mughadiban*, meaning *muraghiman* (in resentment).

Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he went off in anger at his Lord. This was preferred by Ibn Jarir, al-Qutaybi and al-Mahdawi. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud [...]. al-Nahhas said: "Some who do not know the language may deny this, but it is a correct view. The meaning is: angry on account of his Lord, just as you say *ghadibtu laka*, meaning: on your account." Al-Dahhak said: he went off in anger at his people. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas [...]. A group among them, including al-Akhfash, said: he only left in anger at the king who was in his time, whose name was Hizqiya. It has also been said: he was not angry at his Lord, nor at his people, nor at the king, but the word is derived from *ghadiba* meaning "to be disdainful [of something]." That is because when he promised his people punishment and went out from among them, they repented, and God removed the punishment from them. When he returned and realised that they had not been destroyed, he was disdainful of that and left them. Among the uses of *al-ghadab* (anger) in this sense is the words of the poet:

*"And I am disdainful [aghdab] that Tamim be mocked with 'Amir"*

That is, *anaf* (I am offended/disdainful).

﴿So he thought that We would not decree [any hardship] upon him﴾. The majority of readers read *naqdira* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *kasra* on the *dal*. There has been disagreement about the meaning of the verse according to this reading. It has been said that its meaning is that it occurred to him that God Most High would not be able to punish him. This view has been related from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but it is a rejected view, for such an assumption about God is disbelief, and such a thing cannot occur from the prophets, peace be upon them.

The majority of scholars held that its meaning is: *fa-zanna an lan nuḍayyiqa 'alayhi* ("he thought that We would not constrict [his provision] upon him"), like His words: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts [it]﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], that is, He constricts it. From this is His words: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted [qudira 'alayhi rizquhu]﴾ [al-Talaq: 7] (p-944). It is said: *qadara*, *qaddara*, *qatara* and *qattara*, meaning: he constricted.

It has also been said that it is from *al-qadar*, which is decree and judgment: that is, *fa-zanna an lan naqḍiya 'alayhi al-'uqūba* ("he thought that We would not decree punishment upon him"). This was said by Qatada and Mujahid, and was preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It is derived from *al-qadar*, which means judgment, not from *al-qudra* (power) and *al-isti'ṭa'a* (ability). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: it is from *al-taqdir*, not from *al-qudra*. It is said of it: *qaddara Allahu laka al-khayra yuqaddiruhu qadaran* ("God decreed good for you"). Tha'lab recited:

*"The evening gatherings of al-Liwa will not return to us ever, as long as the fresh rain pours [abrama al-silm al-nadir]"*

*"Nor will that time that passed return, blessed are You, what You decree [tuqaddiru] with that gratitude"*

That is, what You decree and judge by.

Among the things that support what these [scholars] said is the reading of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Zuhri: *fa-zanna an nuqaddira*, with a *ḍamma* on the *nun* and a *shadda* on the *dal*, from *al-taqdir*. Al-Mawardi related this reading from Ibn 'Abbas. Also supporting this is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Qatada and al-A'raj: *an lan yuqaddara* with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *shadda*, in the passive. Ya'qub, 'Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read *yuqdaru* with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *dal*, unstressed, in the passive.

The scholars have differed on the interpretation of the authentic hadith concerning the man who had done no good deed ever, who told his family to burn him when he died, and then said: "By God, if God constricts [la'in qaddara Allahu 'alayya] [...]" as they differed on the interpretation of this verse. The discussion of this would be lengthy, and we have mentioned here what the reader needs without requiring anything else.

The *fa* in His words ﴿Then he called out in the darknesses﴾ is *faṣīḥa* (explanatory): that is, what happened, namely the fish swallowing him, occurred, and then he called out in the darknesses. By "the darknesses" is meant the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. His call was his words: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾, that is, [saying] that there is no deity except You... The meaning of *subḥānaka* is: glorifying You above anything that could overpower You. ﴿Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾, those who wrong themselves. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: this statement by Yunus is an acknowledgment of his sin and repentance from his wrongdoing, and he said it while he was in the belly of the fish.

Then God, glorified is He, informed that He answered him, saying: ﴿So We responded to him﴾, [answering] his supplication which he made in the course of acknowledging his sin, in the most gentle manner. ﴿And We saved him from the distress﴾, by bringing him out of the belly of the fish until it cast him onto the shore. ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾, that is, We deliver them from their distress through what they had done before and what We have prepared for them of mercy. This is the meaning of the other verse, His words: ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [God], he would have remained within its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143–144].

The majority read *nunji* with two *nun*s. Ibn 'Amir read *nujjī* with a single *nun*, a doubled *jim*, a sukun on the *ya'*, as a past verb with an implied verbal noun (*al-najāh*, "deliverance"), *wa-kadhālika nujjī al-najāta al-mu'minīna*, just as you say *ḍaraba Zaydan*, meaning *ḍaraba al-ḍarba Zaydan* ("he struck the striking, Zayd"). From this is the poet's words:

*"Even if a poor woman gave birth to a dog's puppy, the dogs would curse that puppy"*

This is how al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd and Tha'lab explained the reading. Abu Hatim and al-Zajjaj declared them wrong and said: it is a solecism, for it puts in the accusative the object of a passive verb, whereas it should be *nujjiya al-mu'minūna* ("the believers were delivered").

Abu 'Ubayda had another view, namely that the *nun* was assimilated into the *jim*. al-Qutaybi also held this. al-Nahhas objected to it, saying: "This view is not permissible according to any of the grammarians, because the point of articulation of the *nun* is distant from that of the *jim*, so it is not assimilated into it." Then al-Nahhas said: "I have not heard anything better on this than what I heard from 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash, who said: the original is *nunji*, and one of the two *nun*s was deleted because they came together, just as one of two *ta*s is deleted when they come together, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and do not be divided [wa-la tafarraqu]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], whose original is *wa-la tatafarraqu*."

I say: similarly al-Wahidi, from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, said that the second *nun* is concealed before the *jim* and may not be made clear, so the concealment was mistaken for assimilation, and so he thought it was assimilation. What supports this is that the *ya'* of *najja* is vowelless and the believers are in the accusative. If it were in the passive, the *ya'* would not be vowelless and the believers would have to be in the nominative. I say: we do not accept his statement that it is not permissible to make it clear, for it is made clear in the majority reading.

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu al-'Aliya read ﴿And thus He delivered the believers﴾ in the active voice: that is, God delivered the believers.

Ibn Jarir related from Murra, concerning His words: ﴿when they judged concerning the field﴾, he said: the field was a plant, and sheep grazed in it at night, so they brought the dispute to Dawud, and he ruled that the sheep go to the owners of the field. Then they passed by Sulayman and told him about that. He said: "No, let the sheep be handed over, so they may benefit from them, and these men may tend to their field. When it is as it was, they return them to them." So it was revealed: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾. This has been related from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field﴾, he said: it was a vineyard whose grape clusters had grown, and the sheep destroyed it. Dawud ruled that the sheep go to the owner of the vineyard. Sulayman said: "Other than this, O Prophet of God." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "The vineyard is handed over to the owner of the sheep, so he tends it until it returns as it was, and the sheep are handed to the owner of the vineyard, so he benefits from them. When the vineyard returns as it was, you return the vineyard to its owner and the sheep to their owner." That is His words: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾. 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related similar from Masruq. Ibn Jarir related similar from Ibn 'Abbas, but he did not mention the vineyard. Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, but longer. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: *nafashat* means "grazed."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Maja, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Haram ibn Muhayyisa: "A she-camel of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib entered a garden and damaged it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ruled that the owners of gardens are responsible for guarding them by day, and that what the livestock damages by night is the liability of their owners." This hadith has been criticised, and we have expanded the discussion on it in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*. Ibn Mardawayh related a similar hadith from 'A'isha, and at its end he added: "Then he recited this verse: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾, [to the end of] the verse."

In the *Two Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "While two women were with their two sons, a wolf came and took (p-945) one of the two. They brought their dispute to Dawud, and he ruled for the elder. They went out, and Sulayman called them and said: 'Bring me a knife, I will split it between you.' The younger said: 'May God have mercy on you, he is her son; do not split him.' So he ruled for the younger." Although this hadith is not included in what the verse narrates of their judgment, it is among the events that happened to them.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama* related from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] with Dawud, and the birds﴾, he said: they prayed with Dawud when he prayed. ﴿And We taught him the making of armour for you﴾, he said: they were plates; the first to weave and link them was Dawud, peace be upon him.

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn 'Abbas: Sulayman would have six hundred thousand chairs set out for him. Then the nobles of mankind would come and sit nearest to him. Then the nobles of the jinn would come and sit next to the nobles of mankind. Then he would call the birds, and they would shade them. Then he would call the wind, and it would carry them, travelling a month's distance in a single morning.

Ibn 'Asakir, al-Daylami and Ibn al-Najjar related from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God said to Ayyub: 'Do you know what your offence against Me was, that I tested you?' He said: 'No, O Lord.' He said: 'Because you entered upon Pharaoh and flattered him in two words.'"

Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ayyub's sin was only that a poor man sought his help against an oppressor whom he could have repelled, but he did not help him, nor did he command the good, nor did he forbid the oppressor from oppressing the poor man, so God tested him. In its chain is Juwaybir.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya* related from 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: Ayyub had two brothers who came one day, but they could not bear to draw near to him because of his smell, so they stood at a distance. One of them said to the other: "If God had known any good in Ayyub, He would not have tested him with this." Ayyub was distressed by their words with a distress greater than any he had ever felt. He said: "O God, if You know that I have never spent a night full while I knew where a hungry person was, then confirm me." He was confirmed from the sky while they were listening. Then he said: "O God, if You know that I have never worn a shirt while I knew where a naked person was, then confirm me." He was confirmed from the sky while they were listening. Then he fell prostrate and said: "O God, by Your might, I will not raise my head until You remove it from me." He did not raise his head until God removed it from him.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it through another chain, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with similar wording. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾, that he said: It was said to him, "O Ayyub, your family is yours in Paradise. If you wish, We will bring them to you, and if you wish, We will leave them for you in Paradise." Rather, leave them for Me in Paradise, and in this world you will be given the like of them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: It reached Ibn Mas'ud that Marwan had said regarding this verse, ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾, "He was given a family other than his family." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Rather, he was given his family in their very persons, and the like of them with them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Ruyani, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years. Near and distant people abandoned him, except for two men among his brothers who were among his closest brothers. They used to come to him in the morning and in the evening. One of them said to his companion one day: 'By Allah, you know Ayyub has committed a sin that no one else has committed.' He asked: 'What is that?' He said: 'For eighteen years Allah has not shown him mercy, so He has not removed what afflicts him.' When they went to Ayyub, the man could not restrain himself until he mentioned that to him. Ayyub said: 'I do not know what he is saying, except that Allah knows that I pass by two men quarrelling, mentioning Allah, so I return to my house and expiate for them, out of dislike that Allah should be mentioned except in what is right.' He used to go out for his need, and when he had finished, his wife would take hold of his hand until he reached [his place]. One day she was late with him, so Allah revealed to Ayyub, in his place, ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾ [Sad: 42]. She was slow to come to him, so she met him while he was coming towards her, and Allah had removed from him the affliction that he had, and he was in his best condition. When she saw him she said: 'May Allah bless you! Have you seen the afflicted Prophet of Allah? By Allah, I have never seen a man more like him than you when he was healthy.' He said: 'I am he.'" He had two granaries: a granary for wheat and a granary for barley. Allah sent two clouds. When one of them was over the wheat granary, it poured gold into it until it overflowed, and the other poured silver into the barley granary until it overflowed.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿And Dhu al-Kifl﴾, that he said: "He was a righteous man, not a prophet, who undertook for the prophet of his people that he would take charge of their affairs for him, establish order among them, and judge between them with justice. He did so, and so he was named Dhu al-Kifl (the one of the guarantee)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There was a judge among the Children of Israel, and death came to him. He said: 'Who will take my place on the condition that he does not become angry?' A man said: 'I will.' So he was named Dhu al-Kifl." He mentioned the story. He would pray all night, then in the morning he would stand and judge between the people.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet. Rather, among the Children of Israel there was a righteous man who prayed one hundred prayers every day. When he died, Dhu al-Kifl took on his responsibility after him, and he prayed one hundred prayers every day, so he was named Dhu al-Kifl."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated through the chain of Sa'd, the freed slave of Talhah, from Ibn Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Al-Kifl from the Children of Israel did not refrain from any sin he committed. A woman came to him, and he gave her sixty dinars on condition that he would have intercourse with her. When he sat between her legs as a man sits with his wife, she trembled and wept. He said: 'What makes you weep? Have I forced you?' She said: 'No, but this is an act I have never done before, and only need drove me to it.' He said: 'You do this, and you have never done it? Go, it is yours.' He said: 'By Allah, I will never disobey Allah after this, ever.' He died that same night, and in the morning it was written on his door: 'Indeed, Allah has forgiven al-Kifl.'" al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it through the chain of Sa'd, the freed slave of Talhah.

(p. 946) Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through the chain of Nafi', from Ibn Amr, who said: "In it [the verse] is Dhu al-Kifl."

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger﴾, that he said: "He became angry with his people." ﴿And he thought that We would not have power over him﴾, meaning: that We would not decree a punishment or a trial upon him for what he did to his people in his anger toward them and his fleeing. He said: "His punishment was that the whale seized him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And he thought that We would not have power over him﴾, that he said: "He thought that the punishment that befell him would not seize him."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿And he called out in the darknesses﴾, that he said: "The darkness of the night, the darkness of the belly of the whale, and the darkness of the sea."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The supplication of Dhu al-Nun when he was in the belly of the whale: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." No Muslim has ever called upon his Lord with it concerning anything except that He has responded to him.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The Name of Allah by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives, is the supplication of Yunus ibn Matta.'" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this specific to Yunus, or to the whole community of Muslims?" He said: "It is specific to Yunus, and general for the believers when they call upon Him with it. Have you not heard the words of Allah: ﴿And thus We deliver the believers﴾? So it is a condition from Allah for whoever calls upon Him with it."

al-Hakim narrated a similar report from his (Ibn Abbas's) narration as well. It is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not proper for anyone to say: 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta.'" It is also narrated in the Sahih and elsewhere from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is also narrated in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 21, verses 78–88 (part 1 of 3):

.
His saying: "Dawud" is conjoined to "Nuh" and is an object governed by its governing verb, either the one mentioned or the one implied, as has passed. "Sulayman" is conjoined to "Dawud." The adverbial phrase in ﴿when they both judged﴾ is connected to what governed "Dawud," meaning: mention them at the time of their judgment. The purpose of mentioning them is to mention their story. The meaning of ﴿concerning the tilth﴾ is "regarding the matter of the tilth." It was said: it was a field of crops; it was said: a vineyard; and the term "harth" (tilth) applies to both. ﴿When the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾ means they scattered and spread out in it. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-nafsh" (with a vowel on the first letter) is when sheep spread out at night without a shepherd. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ means to the judgment of the two judges. In this there is the permissibility of using the plural for two, which is the view of a group of Arabic grammarians such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Radi, and al-Farra' preceded both of them in saying this. It was said: (p-٩٤٢) the intended meaning is the two judges and the one judged against, and "witnesses" means present. The clause is parenthetical.

The clause ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾ is conjoined to "when they both judged," because that is in the sense of the past. The pronoun in "fafahhamnaha" (We gave understanding of it) refers to the matter understood from the speech, or to the judgment indicated by the mention of the ruling.

The exegetes said: two men entered upon Dawud, and with him was his son Sulayman. One of them was the owner of a field, and the other the owner of sheep. The owner of the field said: "This man's sheep got loose at night, entered my field, and left nothing of it." He said: "You are entitled to the sheep as compensation." Sulayman said: "Or something other than that: the owners of the vineyard should take the sheep, benefit from their milk and produce, and the owners of the sheep should tend the vineyard. Then, when it returns to its condition, as on the night the sheep strayed into it, they will return each one's property to its owner." Dawud said: "The judgment is what you have decided," and he ruled accordingly. Al-Nahhas said: Dawud only ruled the sheep for the owner of the field because their price was close to his loss. As for Sulayman's ruling, it was said: the value of what the sheep took and the value of what they destroyed were equal.

A group of scholars said: Dawud judged by revelation, and Sulayman judged by revelation, a revelation by which God abrogated Dawud's ruling. Thus the "understanding" in this view is by way of revelation. The majority said: their judgment was by ijtihad (independent reasoning, the exertion of a qualified jurist to derive a ruling). The discussion of the judgment of the prophets' ijtihad is well known, and likewise what the scholars mentioned concerning the disagreement of mujtahids (qualified jurists exercising ijtihad): is every mujtahid correct, or is the truth with one of them? Those who argue that every mujtahid is correct have cited this verse, but this verse does not indicate that, nor does any other. Rather, the hadith agreed upon in the two Sahihs and others explicitly states that when a judge strives and is correct, he has two rewards, and if he strives and errs, he has one reward. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, called him "mistaken" (mukhti', one who errs). So how can it be said that he is correct in matching the judgment of God? For the judgment of God, Glorified is He, is one and does not differ according to the differences of mujtahids. Otherwise it would follow that His judgment depends on the ijtihad of mujtahids, and the implication is false, so the implicating thing is likewise false. Also it would be implied that the thing concerning which the mujtahids differed as to its being lawful or unlawful is lawful in the judgment of God, Glorified is He. This implication: every mujtahid has an ijtihad in that case, and what God, Glorified is He, wills concerning it does not end except with the end of the mujtahids. The implication is false, so the implicating thing is likewise false. We have clarified this question with what has no addition to it in the work we named "al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid" (The Beneficial Word on the Ruling of Taqlid) and "Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab" (The Etiquette of Seeking and the Final Aim). Whoever wishes to verify the truth should refer to those two.

If you say: what is the ruling of this incident, in which Dawud and Sulayman judged, under this Muhammadan Shari'ah and the Islamic religion? I say: it has been established from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, through the hadith of al-Bara' that he legislated for his community that the owners of livestock must guard them at night, and the owners of orchards must guard them by day, and that what livestock destroy at night is a liability upon their owners. This liability is the amount of what was lost, either in kind or in value. The majority of scholars have acted upon what this hadith contains. Abu Hanifa, his companions, and a group of the Kufans held that this ruling was abrogated, and that when animals destroy crops by night or by day, their owner is not obligated to anything. They included the destruction of animals within the generality of the Prophet's saying, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: "The wound caused by an animal is unpaid" (jurh al-'ajma' jubar), analogizing all of their actions to their wounding (qiyas, analogical reasoning). It is answered that this analogy is invalid, because it stands against the explicit text. Some scholars held that the owner of the livestock is liable for what they destroy, without distinction between night and day. It is answered by the hadith of al-Bara'. And among what indicates that these two rulings of Dawud and Sulayman were by revelation from God, Glorified is He, and not by ijtihad, is the following.

His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. God, Glorified is He, informed us that He gave each of them these two matters. If they are specific, then their applicability to this case which God related about them takes precedence over their applicability to other cases. If they are general, then this instance of judgment and knowledge, which occurred from each of them in this case, is the most appropriate of the individual cases of that general term to be included under it and to be indicated by it. From this it is derived that what might be suggested by specifying Sulayman with understanding is dispelled, namely that Dawud's ruling was not a legal ruling. That is: each of them We gave judgment and abundant knowledge, not Sulayman alone.

When He praised Dawud and Sulayman together, He then mentioned what is specific to each of them. He began with Dawud, saying: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] with Dawud﴾. The glorification (tasbih) is either literal or figurative. A group held the first view, and it is the apparent meaning. That is because when Dawud glorified, the mountains glorified with him. It was said that they prayed with him when he prayed, and that is the meaning of glorification. Another group held the figurative view and interpreted the glorification as the glorification of one who sees them in wonder at the greatness of their creation and the power of their Creator. It was said that the mountains would move with Dawud, and whoever saw them moving with him glorified God. "And the birds" is conjoined to "the mountains." It is also read in the nominative, as a subject with an omitted predicate: "and the birds are subjected." Conjunction to the pronoun in "yusabbihna" is not valid, because there is no emphasis and no separation. ﴿And We were ever doers﴾ means what has been mentioned: the giving of understanding, the bestowing of judgment, and the subjugation.

﴿And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail for you﴾. Al-labus, in the Arabs' usage, is all weaponry, whether a coat of mail, a cuirass, a sword, or a spear. Al-Hudhali said: "And with me is a labus among garments, as if it were..." etc. The meaning in the verse is specifically coats of mail, and it is in the sense of "the thing worn," like "rakub" (ridden) and "halub" (milked). The prepositional phrase "for you" is connected to "We taught." ﴿That He might protect you from your violence﴾. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, and Rawh read "li-tuhassinakum" with the letter ta' on top, referring the pronoun to the craft, or to "labus" with the interpretation of "the coat of mail." Shayba, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "li-nuhassinakum" with nun, referring the pronoun to Him, Glorified is He. The rest read with ya', referring the pronoun to "labus," or to Dawud, or to God, Glorified is He. The meaning of "min ba'sikum" is "from your war," or "from the striking of weapons upon you." ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ for this blessing which We have bestowed upon you. The interrogative is in the sense of a command.

Then He mentioned what was specific to Sulayman. He said: ﴿And to Sulayman the wind﴾. That is, We subjected to him the wind, violent, that is, strong in its blowing. It is said: "the wind became violent," meaning it grew strong, so it is a violent wind (rih 'asif) and 'asuf. The accusative of "al-rih" is by way of circumstance. 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, al-Sulami, and Abu Bakr read "wa-li-Sulayman al-rihu" with the nominative on "al-rih," as a new beginning, and it is the subject with its predicate "tajri" (runs). As for the reading of the accusative, the position of "tajri bi-amrihi" (it runs by his command) is also accusative, as a circumstance or as a substitute, ﴿to the land which We had blessed﴾, which is the land of Syria, as has passed before. ﴿And We were ever knowing of all things﴾, that is, of the destruction of every thing.

﴿And of the devils﴾, that is, We subjected from among the devils those who dive for him in the seas and bring up from them what he sought from them. It was said that "min" is a subject whose predicate is what precedes it. Diving (al-ghawsh) is descending beneath the water; one says "ghasa fi al-ma'" (he dived into the water), and a ghawwas is one who dives in the sea for pearls. ﴿And they did works other than that﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, other than that. It was said: he meant by that the prayer niches (mahareeb), statues, and other things for which he subjected them. ﴿And We were ever guardians over them﴾, that is, over their works. Al-Farra' said: guarding them from fleeing or from refusing, or We guarded them from departing from His command. Al-Zajjaj said: He used to guard them from spoiling what they had done, and their habit was to spoil by night what they had done by day.

﴿And Ayyub, when he called upon his Lord﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and its governing verb is either what is mentioned or what is implied, as has passed. The governing verb of the adverbial phrase, namely "when he called upon his Lord," is the same governing verb of Ayyub. ﴿That harm has touched me﴾, that is, "that harm has touched me." It was read with the kasra on "inni." ﴿The harm which befell him is disputed: it was said that he got up to pray and could not rise. It was said that he acknowledged his incapacity, so that this would not contradict patience. It was said that revelation was cut off from him for forty days. It was said that a worm fell from his flesh, and he picked it up and returned it to its place, and it ate from him, so he cried out "harm has touched me." It was said that worms took hold of his body, and he endured until a worm reached his heart. It was said that his harm was the saying of Iblis to his wife: "Prostrate to me," and he feared the loss of her faith. It was said that his people loathed him. It was said that by harm he meant mockery. It was said other than that.

When he called upon his Lord humbly, he described Him with the utmost mercy, saying: ﴿And You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾. So God, Glorified is He, informed of His responding to his supplication, saying: ﴿So We responded to him, and removed what harm was upon him﴾, that is, God healed him of what he had, and compensated him for what he had lost. For this reason He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. It was said that God left them for him and gave him the like of them in this world. Al-Nahhas said: the attribution of this is correct, and his family had all died except his wife, so God restored them in less than the blink of an eye, and gave him the like of them along with them. It was said that this was by his having a number of children double those whom God had caused to die, so the meaning of the verse according to this is: We gave him the like of his family and the like of them with them. The accusative of ﴿a mercy from Us﴾ is by way of cause: that is, We gave him that out of Our mercy to him. ﴿And a reminder for the worshippers﴾, that is, and a reminder to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient. It is disputed how long he remained under the affliction: it was said seven years, seven months, seven days, and seven nights; it was said thirty years; it was said eighteen years.

﴿And Isma'il, and Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl﴾, that is, mention these. Idris is Enoch (Akhnukh), and Dhu al-Kifl is Ilyas (Elias). It was said he was Yusha' ibn Nun, it was said Zakariyya. The correct view is that he was a man from the Children of Israel who did not refrain from any of the sins, then he repented, and God forgave him. It was said that when al-Yasa' grew old he said: "Who will undertake for me such and such of the qualities of good, so that I may appoint him as my successor?" A man said: "I will." So he appointed him, and he was named Dhu al-Kifl. It was said he was a man who would take responsibility for the affairs of every person when he fell into any of the important matters. It was said other than that. The majority have held that he was not a prophet, and a group said he was a prophet. Then God, Glorified is He, described these by patience, saying: ﴿Each of them was of the patient﴾, that is, each one of these was among the patient in carrying out what God had obligated them to.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 21, verses 78–88 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾, that is, into Paradise, or into prophethood, or into goodness in its general sense. Then he gave the reason for that in His words: ﴿Indeed, they were among the righteous﴾, that is, those perfect in righteousness.

And [mention] Dhu al-Nun (Dhu al-Nun, "the man of the fish"), that is, mention Dhu al-Nun, who is Yunus ibn Matta. He was given the title Dhu al-Nun because the fish swallowed him, for *al-nun* is one of the names of the fish. It has also been said that he was called Dhu al-Nun because he saw a beautiful child and said: "Make his *nunah* dark, lest the evil eye afflict him." Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that the *nunah* of a child is the soft spot found on the chin of a small child. The meaning of *dassimu* ("make dark") is *sawwidu* ("blacken"). ﴿When he went off in anger﴾, that is, mention Dhu al-Nun at the time when he went off *mughadiban*, meaning *muraghiman* (in resentment).

Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he went off in anger at his Lord. This was preferred by Ibn Jarir, al-Qutaybi and al-Mahdawi. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud [...]. al-Nahhas said: "Some who do not know the language may deny this, but it is a correct view. The meaning is: angry on account of his Lord, just as you say *ghadibtu laka*, meaning: on your account." Al-Dahhak said: he went off in anger at his people. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas [...]. A group among them, including al-Akhfash, said: he only left in anger at the king who was in his time, whose name was Hizqiya. It has also been said: he was not angry at his Lord, nor at his people, nor at the king, but the word is derived from *ghadiba* meaning "to be disdainful [of something]." That is because when he promised his people punishment and went out from among them, they repented, and God removed the punishment from them. When he returned and realised that they had not been destroyed, he was disdainful of that and left them. Among the uses of *al-ghadab* (anger) in this sense is the words of the poet:

*"And I am disdainful [aghdab] that Tamim be mocked with 'Amir"*

That is, *anaf* (I am offended/disdainful).

﴿So he thought that We would not decree [any hardship] upon him﴾. The majority of readers read *naqdira* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *kasra* on the *dal*. There has been disagreement about the meaning of the verse according to this reading. It has been said that its meaning is that it occurred to him that God Most High would not be able to punish him. This view has been related from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but it is a rejected view, for such an assumption about God is disbelief, and such a thing cannot occur from the prophets, peace be upon them.

The majority of scholars held that its meaning is: *fa-zanna an lan nuḍayyiqa 'alayhi* ("he thought that We would not constrict [his provision] upon him"), like His words: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts [it]﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], that is, He constricts it. From this is His words: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted [qudira 'alayhi rizquhu]﴾ [al-Talaq: 7] (p-944). It is said: *qadara*, *qaddara*, *qatara* and *qattara*, meaning: he constricted.

It has also been said that it is from *al-qadar*, which is decree and judgment: that is, *fa-zanna an lan naqḍiya 'alayhi al-'uqūba* ("he thought that We would not decree punishment upon him"). This was said by Qatada and Mujahid, and was preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It is derived from *al-qadar*, which means judgment, not from *al-qudra* (power) and *al-isti'ṭa'a* (ability). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: it is from *al-taqdir*, not from *al-qudra*. It is said of it: *qaddara Allahu laka al-khayra yuqaddiruhu qadaran* ("God decreed good for you"). Tha'lab recited:

*"The evening gatherings of al-Liwa will not return to us ever, as long as the fresh rain pours [abrama al-silm al-nadir]"*

*"Nor will that time that passed return, blessed are You, what You decree [tuqaddiru] with that gratitude"*

That is, what You decree and judge by.

Among the things that support what these [scholars] said is the reading of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Zuhri: *fa-zanna an nuqaddira*, with a *ḍamma* on the *nun* and a *shadda* on the *dal*, from *al-taqdir*. Al-Mawardi related this reading from Ibn 'Abbas. Also supporting this is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Qatada and al-A'raj: *an lan yuqaddara* with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *shadda*, in the passive. Ya'qub, 'Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read *yuqdaru* with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *dal*, unstressed, in the passive.

The scholars have differed on the interpretation of the authentic hadith concerning the man who had done no good deed ever, who told his family to burn him when he died, and then said: "By God, if God constricts [la'in qaddara Allahu 'alayya] [...]" as they differed on the interpretation of this verse. The discussion of this would be lengthy, and we have mentioned here what the reader needs without requiring anything else.

The *fa* in His words ﴿Then he called out in the darknesses﴾ is *faṣīḥa* (explanatory): that is, what happened, namely the fish swallowing him, occurred, and then he called out in the darknesses. By "the darknesses" is meant the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. His call was his words: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾, that is, [saying] that there is no deity except You... The meaning of *subḥānaka* is: glorifying You above anything that could overpower You. ﴿Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾, those who wrong themselves. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: this statement by Yunus is an acknowledgment of his sin and repentance from his wrongdoing, and he said it while he was in the belly of the fish.

Then God, glorified is He, informed that He answered him, saying: ﴿So We responded to him﴾, [answering] his supplication which he made in the course of acknowledging his sin, in the most gentle manner. ﴿And We saved him from the distress﴾, by bringing him out of the belly of the fish until it cast him onto the shore. ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾, that is, We deliver them from their distress through what they had done before and what We have prepared for them of mercy. This is the meaning of the other verse, His words: ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [God], he would have remained within its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143–144].

The majority read *nunji* with two *nun*s. Ibn 'Amir read *nujjī* with a single *nun*, a doubled *jim*, a sukun on the *ya'*, as a past verb with an implied verbal noun (*al-najāh*, "deliverance"), *wa-kadhālika nujjī al-najāta al-mu'minīna*, just as you say *ḍaraba Zaydan*, meaning *ḍaraba al-ḍarba Zaydan* ("he struck the striking, Zayd"). From this is the poet's words:

*"Even if a poor woman gave birth to a dog's puppy, the dogs would curse that puppy"*

This is how al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd and Tha'lab explained the reading. Abu Hatim and al-Zajjaj declared them wrong and said: it is a solecism, for it puts in the accusative the object of a passive verb, whereas it should be *nujjiya al-mu'minūna* ("the believers were delivered").

Abu 'Ubayda had another view, namely that the *nun* was assimilated into the *jim*. al-Qutaybi also held this. al-Nahhas objected to it, saying: "This view is not permissible according to any of the grammarians, because the point of articulation of the *nun* is distant from that of the *jim*, so it is not assimilated into it." Then al-Nahhas said: "I have not heard anything better on this than what I heard from 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash, who said: the original is *nunji*, and one of the two *nun*s was deleted because they came together, just as one of two *ta*s is deleted when they come together, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and do not be divided [wa-la tafarraqu]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], whose original is *wa-la tatafarraqu*."

I say: similarly al-Wahidi, from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, said that the second *nun* is concealed before the *jim* and may not be made clear, so the concealment was mistaken for assimilation, and so he thought it was assimilation. What supports this is that the *ya'* of *najja* is vowelless and the believers are in the accusative. If it were in the passive, the *ya'* would not be vowelless and the believers would have to be in the nominative. I say: we do not accept his statement that it is not permissible to make it clear, for it is made clear in the majority reading.

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu al-'Aliya read ﴿And thus He delivered the believers﴾ in the active voice: that is, God delivered the believers.

Ibn Jarir related from Murra, concerning His words: ﴿when they judged concerning the field﴾, he said: the field was a plant, and sheep grazed in it at night, so they brought the dispute to Dawud, and he ruled that the sheep go to the owners of the field. Then they passed by Sulayman and told him about that. He said: "No, let the sheep be handed over, so they may benefit from them, and these men may tend to their field. When it is as it was, they return them to them." So it was revealed: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾. This has been related from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field﴾, he said: it was a vineyard whose grape clusters had grown, and the sheep destroyed it. Dawud ruled that the sheep go to the owner of the vineyard. Sulayman said: "Other than this, O Prophet of God." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "The vineyard is handed over to the owner of the sheep, so he tends it until it returns as it was, and the sheep are handed to the owner of the vineyard, so he benefits from them. When the vineyard returns as it was, you return the vineyard to its owner and the sheep to their owner." That is His words: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾. 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related similar from Masruq. Ibn Jarir related similar from Ibn 'Abbas, but he did not mention the vineyard. Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, but longer. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: *nafashat* means "grazed."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Maja, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Haram ibn Muhayyisa: "A she-camel of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib entered a garden and damaged it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ruled that the owners of gardens are responsible for guarding them by day, and that what the livestock damages by night is the liability of their owners." This hadith has been criticised, and we have expanded the discussion on it in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*. Ibn Mardawayh related a similar hadith from 'A'isha, and at its end he added: "Then he recited this verse: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾, [to the end of] the verse."

In the *Two Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "While two women were with their two sons, a wolf came and took (p-945) one of the two. They brought their dispute to Dawud, and he ruled for the elder. They went out, and Sulayman called them and said: 'Bring me a knife, I will split it between you.' The younger said: 'May God have mercy on you, he is her son; do not split him.' So he ruled for the younger." Although this hadith is not included in what the verse narrates of their judgment, it is among the events that happened to them.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama* related from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] with Dawud, and the birds﴾, he said: they prayed with Dawud when he prayed. ﴿And We taught him the making of armour for you﴾, he said: they were plates; the first to weave and link them was Dawud, peace be upon him.

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn 'Abbas: Sulayman would have six hundred thousand chairs set out for him. Then the nobles of mankind would come and sit nearest to him. Then the nobles of the jinn would come and sit next to the nobles of mankind. Then he would call the birds, and they would shade them. Then he would call the wind, and it would carry them, travelling a month's distance in a single morning.

Ibn 'Asakir, al-Daylami and Ibn al-Najjar related from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God said to Ayyub: 'Do you know what your offence against Me was, that I tested you?' He said: 'No, O Lord.' He said: 'Because you entered upon Pharaoh and flattered him in two words.'"

Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ayyub's sin was only that a poor man sought his help against an oppressor whom he could have repelled, but he did not help him, nor did he command the good, nor did he forbid the oppressor from oppressing the poor man, so God tested him. In its chain is Juwaybir.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya* related from 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: Ayyub had two brothers who came one day, but they could not bear to draw near to him because of his smell, so they stood at a distance. One of them said to the other: "If God had known any good in Ayyub, He would not have tested him with this." Ayyub was distressed by their words with a distress greater than any he had ever felt. He said: "O God, if You know that I have never spent a night full while I knew where a hungry person was, then confirm me." He was confirmed from the sky while they were listening. Then he said: "O God, if You know that I have never worn a shirt while I knew where a naked person was, then confirm me." He was confirmed from the sky while they were listening. Then he fell prostrate and said: "O God, by Your might, I will not raise my head until You remove it from me." He did not raise his head until God removed it from him.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it through another chain, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with similar wording. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾, that he said: It was said to him, "O Ayyub, your family is yours in Paradise. If you wish, We will bring them to you, and if you wish, We will leave them for you in Paradise." Rather, leave them for Me in Paradise, and in this world you will be given the like of them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: It reached Ibn Mas'ud that Marwan had said regarding this verse, ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾, "He was given a family other than his family." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Rather, he was given his family in their very persons, and the like of them with them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Ruyani, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years. Near and distant people abandoned him, except for two men among his brothers who were among his closest brothers. They used to come to him in the morning and in the evening. One of them said to his companion one day: 'By Allah, you know Ayyub has committed a sin that no one else has committed.' He asked: 'What is that?' He said: 'For eighteen years Allah has not shown him mercy, so He has not removed what afflicts him.' When they went to Ayyub, the man could not restrain himself until he mentioned that to him. Ayyub said: 'I do not know what he is saying, except that Allah knows that I pass by two men quarrelling, mentioning Allah, so I return to my house and expiate for them, out of dislike that Allah should be mentioned except in what is right.' He used to go out for his need, and when he had finished, his wife would take hold of his hand until he reached [his place]. One day she was late with him, so Allah revealed to Ayyub, in his place, ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾ [Sad: 42]. She was slow to come to him, so she met him while he was coming towards her, and Allah had removed from him the affliction that he had, and he was in his best condition. When she saw him she said: 'May Allah bless you! Have you seen the afflicted Prophet of Allah? By Allah, I have never seen a man more like him than you when he was healthy.' He said: 'I am he.'" He had two granaries: a granary for wheat and a granary for barley. Allah sent two clouds. When one of them was over the wheat granary, it poured gold into it until it overflowed, and the other poured silver into the barley granary until it overflowed.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿And Dhu al-Kifl﴾, that he said: "He was a righteous man, not a prophet, who undertook for the prophet of his people that he would take charge of their affairs for him, establish order among them, and judge between them with justice. He did so, and so he was named Dhu al-Kifl (the one of the guarantee)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There was a judge among the Children of Israel, and death came to him. He said: 'Who will take my place on the condition that he does not become angry?' A man said: 'I will.' So he was named Dhu al-Kifl." He mentioned the story. He would pray all night, then in the morning he would stand and judge between the people.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet. Rather, among the Children of Israel there was a righteous man who prayed one hundred prayers every day. When he died, Dhu al-Kifl took on his responsibility after him, and he prayed one hundred prayers every day, so he was named Dhu al-Kifl."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated through the chain of Sa'd, the freed slave of Talhah, from Ibn Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Al-Kifl from the Children of Israel did not refrain from any sin he committed. A woman came to him, and he gave her sixty dinars on condition that he would have intercourse with her. When he sat between her legs as a man sits with his wife, she trembled and wept. He said: 'What makes you weep? Have I forced you?' She said: 'No, but this is an act I have never done before, and only need drove me to it.' He said: 'You do this, and you have never done it? Go, it is yours.' He said: 'By Allah, I will never disobey Allah after this, ever.' He died that same night, and in the morning it was written on his door: 'Indeed, Allah has forgiven al-Kifl.'" al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it through the chain of Sa'd, the freed slave of Talhah.

(p. 946) Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through the chain of Nafi', from Ibn Amr, who said: "In it [the verse] is Dhu al-Kifl."

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger﴾, that he said: "He became angry with his people." ﴿And he thought that We would not have power over him﴾, meaning: that We would not decree a punishment or a trial upon him for what he did to his people in his anger toward them and his fleeing. He said: "His punishment was that the whale seized him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And he thought that We would not have power over him﴾, that he said: "He thought that the punishment that befell him would not seize him."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿And he called out in the darknesses﴾, that he said: "The darkness of the night, the darkness of the belly of the whale, and the darkness of the sea."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The supplication of Dhu al-Nun when he was in the belly of the whale: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." No Muslim has ever called upon his Lord with it concerning anything except that He has responded to him.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The Name of Allah by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives, is the supplication of Yunus ibn Matta.'" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this specific to Yunus, or to the whole community of Muslims?" He said: "It is specific to Yunus, and general for the believers when they call upon Him with it. Have you not heard the words of Allah: ﴿And thus We deliver the believers﴾? So it is a condition from Allah for whoever calls upon Him with it."

al-Hakim narrated a similar report from his (Ibn Abbas's) narration as well. It is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not proper for anyone to say: 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta.'" It is also narrated in the Sahih and elsewhere from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is also narrated in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 21, verses 78–88 (part 1 of 3):

.
His saying: "Dawud" is conjoined to "Nuh" and is an object governed by its governing verb, either the one mentioned or the one implied, as has passed. "Sulayman" is conjoined to "Dawud." The adverbial phrase in ﴿when they both judged﴾ is connected to what governed "Dawud," meaning: mention them at the time of their judgment. The purpose of mentioning them is to mention their story. The meaning of ﴿concerning the tilth﴾ is "regarding the matter of the tilth." It was said: it was a field of crops; it was said: a vineyard; and the term "harth" (tilth) applies to both. ﴿When the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾ means they scattered and spread out in it. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-nafsh" (with a vowel on the first letter) is when sheep spread out at night without a shepherd. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ means to the judgment of the two judges. In this there is the permissibility of using the plural for two, which is the view of a group of Arabic grammarians such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Radi, and al-Farra' preceded both of them in saying this. It was said: (p-٩٤٢) the intended meaning is the two judges and the one judged against, and "witnesses" means present. The clause is parenthetical.

The clause ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾ is conjoined to "when they both judged," because that is in the sense of the past. The pronoun in "fafahhamnaha" (We gave understanding of it) refers to the matter understood from the speech, or to the judgment indicated by the mention of the ruling.

The exegetes said: two men entered upon Dawud, and with him was his son Sulayman. One of them was the owner of a field, and the other the owner of sheep. The owner of the field said: "This man's sheep got loose at night, entered my field, and left nothing of it." He said: "You are entitled to the sheep as compensation." Sulayman said: "Or something other than that: the owners of the vineyard should take the sheep, benefit from their milk and produce, and the owners of the sheep should tend the vineyard. Then, when it returns to its condition, as on the night the sheep strayed into it, they will return each one's property to its owner." Dawud said: "The judgment is what you have decided," and he ruled accordingly. Al-Nahhas said: Dawud only ruled the sheep for the owner of the field because their price was close to his loss. As for Sulayman's ruling, it was said: the value of what the sheep took and the value of what they destroyed were equal.

A group of scholars said: Dawud judged by revelation, and Sulayman judged by revelation, a revelation by which God abrogated Dawud's ruling. Thus the "understanding" in this view is by way of revelation. The majority said: their judgment was by ijtihad (independent reasoning, the exertion of a qualified jurist to derive a ruling). The discussion of the judgment of the prophets' ijtihad is well known, and likewise what the scholars mentioned concerning the disagreement of mujtahids (qualified jurists exercising ijtihad): is every mujtahid correct, or is the truth with one of them? Those who argue that every mujtahid is correct have cited this verse, but this verse does not indicate that, nor does any other. Rather, the hadith agreed upon in the two Sahihs and others explicitly states that when a judge strives and is correct, he has two rewards, and if he strives and errs, he has one reward. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, called him "mistaken" (mukhti', one who errs). So how can it be said that he is correct in matching the judgment of God? For the judgment of God, Glorified is He, is one and does not differ according to the differences of mujtahids. Otherwise it would follow that His judgment depends on the ijtihad of mujtahids, and the implication is false, so the implicating thing is likewise false. Also it would be implied that the thing concerning which the mujtahids differed as to its being lawful or unlawful is lawful in the judgment of God, Glorified is He. This implication: every mujtahid has an ijtihad in that case, and what God, Glorified is He, wills concerning it does not end except with the end of the mujtahids. The implication is false, so the implicating thing is likewise false.
